nodes.statement_short: Show $y,z\in\mathrm{im}(F)$ so $x$ is divisible by $p$.

nodes.name: $y$ lies in the image of $F$
nodes.statement: First, $-dx \equiv d((F-1) x)$ modulo $p$, so $dx$ is divisible by $p$. It follows that $d Vy$, and hence $dy = FdVy$ is divisible by $p$, so that $y$ belongs to the image of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: $dx$ divisible by $p$ forces $y\in\mathrm{im}F$.

nodes.name: $z$ lies in the image of $F$
nodes.statement: In particular, modulo $p$, we have $x \equiv dV z$ and $(F-1) d Vz = d (z - Vz)$ is divisible by $p$. Therefore, $z - Vz$ belongs to the image of $F$. Since the operator $V$ is topologically nilpotent on $W \Omega^n_R$, we find that $(1 - V)$ is invertible and $z \in \mathrm{im}(F)$.
nodes.statement_short: $z-Vz\in\mathrm{im}F$ and $1-V$ is invertible.

nodes.name: Conclude injectivity
nodes.statement: Therefore, $x$ is divisible by $p$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $x$ is divisible by $p$.

nodes.name: Saturated Dieudonn\'e complex
nodes.statement: A \emph{saturated} Dieudonn\'e complex $(X^{\ast}, d, F)$ is a $p$-torsion-free cochain complex equipped with an operator $F: X^{\ast} \to X^{\ast}$ such that $dF = pFd$, the opeartor $F: X^n \to X^n$ is injective, and the image of $F$ consists precisely of those $x \in X^n$ such that $p $ divides $dx$; this implies that one can define uniquely an operator $V$ such that $FV = VF = p$.

nodes.name: Strict Dieudonn\'e complex
nodes.statement: A saturated Dieudonn\'e complex $(X^{\ast}, d, F)$ is called \emph{strict} if $X^{\ast}$ is in addition complete for the filtration defined by $\{\mathrm{im}(V^n, d V^n)\}$.

nodes.name: Kernel and cokernel of $F-1$ on strict Dieudonn\'e complexes commute with filtered colimits
nodes.statement: The functors from the category of strict Dieudonn\'e complexes to graded abelian groups given by $$(X^{\ast}, d, F)\mapsto \mathrm{ker}(F-1: X^{\ast}/p \to X^{\ast}/p), \quad \mathrm{coker}( F-1 : X^{\ast}/p \to X^{\ast}/p) $$ commute with filtered colimits.
conclusions: The functors from the category of strict Dieudonn\'e complexes to graded abelian groups given by
commute with filtered colimits
nodes.label: strictDieudonne

nodes.name: Proof sketch for strict Dieudonn\'e complexes
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{strictDieudonne} can be proved in an entirely analogous manner as above.
nodes.statement_short: Argue exactly as for de Rham--Witt complexes of ind-smooth algebras.

nodes.name: Nonunital $R$-algebra
nodes.statement: Given a commutative base ring $R$, a \emph{nonunital $R$-algebra} is an $R$-module $I$ equipped with a multiplication map $I \otimes_R I \to I$ which is commutative and associative. We denote the category of nonunital $R$-algebras by $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. By contrast, when we say ``$R$-algebra,'' we assume the existence of a unit.
differentia: equipped with a multiplication map $I \otimes_R I \to I$ which is commutative and associative

nodes.name: Unitalization $R \ltimes J$
nodes.statement: Conversely, given a nonunital $R$-algebra $J$, we can adjoin to it a unit and thus form the $R$-algebra $S = R \ltimes J$, in which $J$ is embedded as an ideal.

nodes.name: Nonunital algebras are augmented algebras
nodes.statement: This latter construction establishes an equivalence between the category of nonunital $R$-algebras and the category of augmented $R$-algebras.
conclusions: This latter construction establishes an equivalence between the category of nonunital $R$-algebras and the category of augmented $R$-algebras

nodes.name: Free nonunital algebra on $n$ generators
nodes.statement: Let $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+$ denote the ideal $(x_1, \dots, x_n) \subset R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ in the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. Then $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+$ is the free object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ on $n$ generators.

nodes.name: Short exact sequence of nonunital algebras
nodes.statement: We say that a sequence $I' \to I \to \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ is a \emph{short exact sequence} if it is a short exact sequence of underlying abelian groups. That is, $I \to \overline{I}$ is surjective, and we can recover $I'$ as the pullback $0 \times_{\overline{I}} I$ in the category $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$.

nodes.name: Local nonunital algebra
nodes.statement: A non-unital $R$-algebra $I$ is \emph{local} if the following equivalent conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item For any $x \in I$, there exists $y \in I$ (necessarily unique) such that $x + y + xy = 0$. \item Whenever $I$ embeds as an ideal in an $R$-algebra $S$, then $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $S$. \item $I \subset R \ltimes I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $R \ltimes I$. \end{enumerate} The equivalence of the above conditions follows because, given an ideal $I \subset S$ in a commutative ring $S$, then $I$ belongs to the Jacobson radical of $S$ if and only if $1 + I$ consists of units of $S$. We let $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ denote the full subcategory of nonunital local $R$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: $I$ is local if $1+I$ consists of units, i.e. $I$ lies in the Jacobson radical of $R\ltimes I$.

nodes.name: Localization $I[(1+I)^{-1}]$ of a nonunital algebra
nodes.statement: Namely, given a nonunital $R$-algebra $I$, we can build a local nonunital $R$-algebra $I[(1+I)^{-1}]$ as follows: the elements formally written $``1+x"$ for $x\in I$ form a commutative monoid under multiplication, and this monoid acts on $I$ by multiplication. This makes $I$ into a non-unital algebra over the monoid ring $R[1+I]$, and we can set \begin{equation} I[(1+I)^{-1}] := I\otimes_{R[1+I]} R[(1+I)^{gp}], \end{equation} where $(1+I)^{gp}$ is the group completion.
nodes.statement_short: Invert the monoid $1+I$ acting on $I$ to get the local nonunital algebra $I[(1+I)^{-1}]$.

nodes.name: Free local nonunital algebra
nodes.statement: Let $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)}\in\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$ be the image of $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+\in\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ under the left adjoint explained above. In other words, $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)}$ is the ideal $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of the localization $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]_{1 + (x_1, \dots, x_n)}$ of the polynomial ring $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ at its multiplicative subset $1 + (x_1, \dots, x_n)$. It follows that $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+_{(x_1, \dots, x_n)}$ is a local nonunital $R$-algebra, and it is the free object on $n$ generators.

nodes.name: Local nonunital algebras as an orthogonal localization
nodes.statement: Stated more formally, the preceding discussion shows that the inclusion $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ is the right adjoint of a \emph{localization} functor on the category $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. Specifically, $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$ consists of those objects in $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ which are orthogonal \cite[Sec. 5.4]{Borceux1} to the map $R[x]^+ \to R[x]^+_{1 + (x)}$, in the sense that such that any map $R[x]^+ \to I$ extends uniquely over $R[x]^+_{1 + (x)}$. Moreover, one sees easily from the construction of the localization \eqref{loccons} that it is independent of the ground ring $R$. Analogous statements will be true when we restrict further to the subcategory of henselian nonunital rings; see the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma_nuh}.

nodes.name: Henselian nonunital algebra
nodes.statement: A nonunital $R$-algebra $I$ is \emph{henselian} if for every $n \geq 1$ and every polynomial $g(x) \in I[x]$, the equation \begin{equation} x(1 + x)^{n-1} + g(x) = 0 \end{equation} has a solution in $I$. We let $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ denote the full subcategory of henselian nonunital $R$-algebras.
differentia: for every $n \geq 1$ and every polynomial $g(x) \in I[x]$, the equation
nodes.label: def_hens_nu

nodes.name: Henselian nonunital algebras are local with unique roots
nodes.statement: We note that if $I$ is a henselian nonunital $R$-algebra then: \begin{enumerate} \item Considering the equation $x + xy + y = 0$ for $y \in I$, we find that $I$ is local, i.e., $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$. \item The root of the equation \eqref{henseq} is necessarily unique: denoting the equation by $f(x)=0$ for simplicity, if $\alpha, \alpha' \in I$ are both roots then we have $f'(\alpha) \in 1 + I$ and so the Taylor expansion shows that $$0 = f(\alpha) - f(\alpha') \in \alpha - \alpha' + I(\alpha - \alpha'),$$ whence $\alpha = \alpha'$ since $I$ is local. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Limits and sifted colimits of henselian nonunital rings
nodes.statement: Since the solution of \eqref{henseq} is unique if it exists, the category of henselian nonunital rings has all limits and sifted colimits, both of which are computed at the level of underlying sets.
conclusions: the category of henselian nonunital rings has all limits and sifted colimits, both of which are computed at the level of underlying sets

nodes.name: Quotients of henselian nonunital algebras are henselian
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $I \twoheadrightarrow I'$ is a surjection in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ and $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$, then $I' \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ too.
assumptions: $I \twoheadrightarrow I'$ is a surjection in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ and $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$
conclusions: $I' \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ too

nodes.name: Henselianity is independent of the base ring
nodes.statement: Finally, the condition that a nonunital $R$-algebra be henselian does not depend on the base ring $R$, i.e., we might as well take $R = \mathbb{Z}$ in the definition.
conclusions: the condition that a nonunital $R$-algebra be henselian does not depend on the base ring $R$

nodes.name: Henselization of nonunital algebras
nodes.statement: Now we prove the existence of a left adjoint $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R \to \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$, which will be called \emph{henselization}.

nodes.name: Existence of nonunital henselization
nodes.statement: The category $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is presentable and the inclusion $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ admits a left adjoint.
conclusions: The category $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is presentable
the inclusion $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ admits a left adjoint
nodes.label: lemma_nuh

nodes.name: Proof of Existence of nonunital henselization
nodes.statement: It follows from the above discussion that $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is the orthogonal \cite[Sec.~5.4]{Borceux1} of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ with respect to the maps \[ f_{n,t}: R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ \to R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ),\] for $n, t \geq 1$. That is, a given object $X \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ belongs to $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ if and only \begin{equation} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R}( R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ), X) \xrightarrow{\cdot\circ f_{n,t}} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R}(R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ , X) \end{equation} is an isomorphism for all $n,t\ge1$. It now follows formally that $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is presentable and the desired left adjoint exists \cite[Cor. 5.4.8]{Borceux1}. Alternatively, one can appeal to the theory of henselian pairs and define the left adjoint directly by taking the henselization of the pair $(R \ltimes I, I)$; see the forthcoming Construction \ref{construction_henselization}.
nodes.statement_short: Express henselian nonunital algebras as an orthogonality class and apply Borceux's reflection theorem.

nodes.name: Orthogonality class
nodes.statement: It follows from the above discussion that $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is the orthogonal \cite[Sec.~5.4]{Borceux1} of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ with respect to the maps \[ f_{n,t}: R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ \to R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ),\] for $n, t \geq 1$. That is, a given object $X \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ belongs to $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ if and only \begin{equation} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R}( R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ), X) \xrightarrow{\cdot\circ f_{n,t}} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R}(R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ , X) \end{equation} is an isomorphism for all $n,t\ge1$.
nodes.statement_short: Henselian nonunital algebras are orthogonal to the maps $f_{n,t}$.

nodes.name: Orthogonality condition for henselian nonunital algebras
nodes.statement: \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R}( R[x_0, \dots, x_t, y]^+/( y(1 + y)^{n-1} + x_0 + x_1 y + \dots + x_t y^t ), X) \xrightarrow{\cdot\circ f_{n,t}} \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R}(R[x_0, \dots, x_t]^+ , X)
nodes.label: hommap

nodes.name: Reflection theorem
nodes.statement: It now follows formally that $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is presentable and the desired left adjoint exists \cite[Cor. 5.4.8]{Borceux1}.
nodes.statement_short: Borceux's result gives presentability and the left adjoint.

nodes.name: Alternative via henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Alternatively, one can appeal to the theory of henselian pairs and define the left adjoint directly by taking the henselization of the pair $(R \ltimes I, I)$; see the forthcoming Construction \ref{construction_henselization}.
nodes.statement_short: Define the adjoint by henselizing $(R\ltimes I,I)$.

nodes.name: Free henselian nonunital algebra $R\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}^+$
nodes.statement: Let $R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+\in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ denote the henselization of $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+ \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. By construction, $R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ is the free object on $n$ generators.
nodes.label: freeobjs

nodes.name: Lawvere theories
nodes.statement: The categories $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$, $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,loc}}_R$ and $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ are all examples of models for a {\em Lawvere} or {\em algebraic theory} \cite[Ch.~3]{ARloc} \cite[Ch.~3]{Borceux}. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category satisfying the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item[(Law)] $\mathcal C$ has all limits and colimits, and is equipped with a functor $U \colon \mathcal C\to \mathrm{Sets}$ which is conservative, preserves sifted colimits, and admits a left adjoint $F \colon \mathrm{Sets}\to\mathcal C$. \end{itemize} For example, $\mathcal C$ might be the category of rings, nonunital rings, groups, etc. In this case, one takes for $U$ the forgetful functor taking the underlying set, and its right adjoint $F$ is the free ring, nonunital ring, group, etc.~on the given set. Denoting by $\{1\}$ a one-point set, the element $F(\{1\})$ is therefore both compact projective (i.e., $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(F(\{1\}), \cdot)$ commutes with sifted colimits) and a strong generator (i.e., $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(F(\{1\}), \cdot)$ is faithful and conservative). The {\em free object of $\mathcal C$ on $n$ generators} is by definition $\bigsqcup_nF(\{1\})\simeq F(\{1,\dots,n\})$. By the monadicity theorem, $\mathcal{C}$ is monadic over $\mathrm{Sets}$, via a monad that preserves sifted colimits. Let $\mathcal C'\subset \mathcal C$ be a full subcategory, and assume that $\mathcal C'$ is closed under limits and sifted colimits (in $\mathcal C$) and that the inclusion $\mathcal C'\subset\mathcal C$ is a right adjoint. Then clearly $\mathcal C'$ also satisfies conditions (Law), with $U'$ given by the restriction of $U$ to $\mathcal C'$. Moreover, the free objects of $\mathcal C'$ are given by applying the left adjoint $\mathcal C\to \mathcal C'$ to the free objects of $\mathcal C$. In practice, this is how the ``free objects'' in the above categories are constructed. According to general results of Lawvere theory \cite[Thm.~3.9.1]{Borceux} (in fact, we do not use the results in this paragraph, but the point of view may be helpful), the full subcategory $\mathcal{C}_{\Sigma} \subset \mathcal{C}$ of compact projective objects of $\mathcal{C}$ is the idempotent completion of the full subcategory consisting of the free objects $\left\{\bigsqcup_{n} F(\{1\}) : n \geq 0\right\}$. Furthermore, $\mathcal{C}$ can be identified with the category of presheaves on $\mathcal{C}_\Sigma$ which commute with finite products. In particular, objects of $\mathcal{C}$ can be identified with sets equipped with various ``operations'' arising from maps between the free objects satisfying various relations.
nodes.label: remark_Lawvere

nodes.name: Henselian pair
nodes.statement: A \emph{pair} is the data $(S, I)$ where $S$ is a commutative ring and $I \subset S$ is an ideal. The collection of pairs forms a category in the obvious manner. The pair $(S, I)$ is said to be \emph{henselian} if the following equivalent (cf.~\cite[Tag 09XD]{stacks-project} for the equivalence) conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item Given a polynomial $f(x) \in S[x]$ and a root $\overline{\alpha} \in S/I$ of $\overline{f} \in (S/I)[x]$ with $\overline{f}'(\alpha)$ being a unit of $S/I$, then $\overline \alpha$ lifts to a root $\alpha \in S$ of $f$. Note that the lifted root $\alpha \in S$ is necessarily unique by the same argument as we gave after Definition \ref{def_hens_nu}. \item The ideal $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $S$, and the same condition as (1) holds for \emph{monic} polynomials $f(x) \in S[x]$. \item Given any commutative diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ A \ar[d] \ar[r] & S \ar[d] \\ B \ar[r] \ar@{-->}[ru] & S/I\ }\end{equation} with $A \to B$ \'etale, there exists a lift as in the dotted arrow. \end{enumerate} We may also say that the surjective map $S \to S/I$ is a henselian pair, if there is no risk of confusion. If $S$ is local with maximal ideal $\frak m$, then $S$ is said to be a \emph{henselian local ring} if $(S, \frak m)$ is a henselian pair.
also_stated_at: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $I \subset R$ an ideal. Then $(R, I)$ is said to be a \emph{henselian pair} if given a polynomial $f(x) \in R[x]$ and a root $\overline{\alpha} \in R/I$ of $\overline{f} \in (R/I)[x]$ with $\overline{f}'(\alpha)$ being a unit of $R/I$, then $\overline \alpha$ lifts to a root $\alpha \in R$ of $f$. Examples of henselian pairs include pairs $(R, I)$ where $R$ is $I$-adically complete (by Hensel's lemma) and pairs $(R, I)$ where $I$ is locally nilpotent.
nodes.label: def:henspair

nodes.name: Lifting diagram for henselian pairs
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ A \ar[d] \ar[r] & S \ar[d] \\ B \ar[r] \ar@{-->}[ru] & S/I\ }
nodes.label: lifthens

nodes.name: Uniqueness in the lifting property
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a henselian pair and consider a diagram as in \eqref{lifthens} with $A \to B$ \'etale. Then the lifting is unique. Indeed, given two liftings $f_1, f_2: B \to S$ in \eqref{lifthens}, we have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ B \otimes_A B \ar[d]^m \ar[r]^{f_1 \otimes f_2} & S \ar[d] \\ B \ar[r] & S/I, }\] for $m \colon B \otimes_A B \to B$ the multiplication map. Since $m$ is also \'etale (in fact, the projection on a direct factor), the lifting property again shows that $f_1 \otimes f_2$ factors through $m$, so $f_1 = f_2$.
nodes.label: uniquenessinliftingproperty

nodes.name: Subideals of henselian ideals are henselian
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair and let $J \subset I$ be a subideal. Then $(R, J)$ remains a henselian pair.
conclusions: $(R, J)$ remains a henselian pair
nodes.label: subideal:henspair

nodes.name: Elkik's lifting theorem
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then $S \to S/I$ has the right lifting property with respect to smooth maps. That is, any diagram as in \eqref{lifthens} with $A \to B$ smooth (rather than \'etale) admits a lift as in the dotted arrow.
conclusions: $S \to S/I$ has the right lifting property with respect to smooth maps
nodes.label: elkikthm

nodes.name: Gabber's criterion for henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair. Then $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $I$ is henselian as a nonunital ring.
conclusions: $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $I$ is henselian as a nonunital ring
equivalent_conditions: $I$ is henselian as a nonunital ring
nodes.label: checkhensnonunital

nodes.name: Henselianity depends only on the ideal
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair. Then $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ is a henselian pair.
conclusions: $(S, I)$ is a henselian pair if and only if $(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ is a henselian pair
equivalent_conditions: $(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ is a henselian pair

nodes.name: Henselization of a pair
nodes.statement: Given a pair $(S, I)$, there is a pair $(S^h, I^h)$ and a map $(S, I) \to (S^h, I^h)$, called the \emph{henselization} of the original pair, with the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item $(S^h, I^h)$ is a henselian pair and is the initial henselian pair receiving a map from $(S, I)$. That is, the construction $(S, I) \mapsto (S^h, I^h)$ is the left adjoint to the forgetful functor from henselian pairs to pairs. \item $S^h$ is a filtered colimit of \'etale $S$-algebras and $I^h = I S^h = I \otimes_S S^h$. \item The map $S/I \to S^h/I^h$ is an isomorphism. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: construction_henselization

nodes.name: Recognizing the henselization
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair. Suppose given a factorization $S \to \widetilde{S} \to S/I$ such that $\widetilde{S}$ is a filtered colimit of \'etale $S$-algebras and such that $\widetilde{S} \to S/I$ has the right lifting property with respect to \'etale morphisms (i.e., the surjection $\widetilde{S} \to S/I$ is a henselian pair). Then $(\widetilde{S}, I \widetilde{S})$ is the henselization of $(S, I)$. To see this, consider a henselian pair $(A, J)$ and a map $(S, I) \to (A, J)$. Considering the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ S \ar[d] \ar[r] & \widetilde{S} \ar@{-->}[ld] \ar[r] & S/I \ar[d] \\ A \ar[rr] & & A/J },\] the ind-\'etaleness of $S \to \widetilde{S}$ implies the existence of a \emph{unique} dotted arrow $\widetilde{S} \to A$ making the diagram commute (cf.~Remark~\ref{uniquenessinliftingproperty}). This verifies the universal property of the henselization. In particular, one can construct $(S^h, I^h)$ by appealing to Quillen's small object argument \cite[Th. 2.1.14]{Hovey} to factor $S \to S/I$ as the composite of a filtered colimit of \'etale morphisms and a morphism that has the right lifting property with respect to \'etale morphisms; the universal property of the henselization then constructs it as a functor. Note that in \eqref{lifthens}, it suffices to take $A, B$ finitely generated over $\mathbb{Z}$, by the structure theory for \'etale morphisms.
nodes.label: hensfact

nodes.name: Milnor square
nodes.statement: A \emph{Milnor square} of commutative rings is a diagram \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ S \ar[d] \ar[r]& T \ar[d] \\ S' \ar[r] & T' } \end{equation} such that the vertical arrows are surjective and such that the diagram is both cartesian and cocartesian in the category of commutative rings. It follows in particular that if $I \subset S$, $J \subset T$ are the respective kernels of the vertical maps $S \to S'$, $T \to T'$, then $f|_I : I \stackrel{\simeq}{\to} J$ establishes an isomorphism of the ideals $I$, $J$.
differentia: the diagram is both cartesian and cocartesian in the category of commutative rings
nodes.label: milnorsquare

nodes.name: Milnor square diagram
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ S \ar[d] \ar[r]& T \ar[d] \\ S' \ar[r] & T' }
nodes.label: milnsquare

nodes.name: Henselization preserves Milnor squares
nodes.statement: Consider a Milnor square as in \eqref{milnsquare} with respect to the ideals $I \subset S$, $J \subset T$. Then the henselizations $S^h$, $T^h$ of $S$, $T$ along $I$, $J$ fit into a Milnor square \[ \xymatrix{ S^h \ar[d] \ar[r] & T^h \ar[d] \\ S' \ar[r] & T' }.\] Furthermore, $T^h \simeq S^h \otimes_S T$.
assumptions: Consider a Milnor square as in \eqref{milnsquare} with respect to the ideals $I \subset S$, $J \subset T$
conclusions: the henselizations $S^h$, $T^h$ of $S$, $T$ along $I$, $J$ fit into a Milnor square
$T^h \simeq S^h \otimes_S T$
nodes.label: milnsquarehens

nodes.name: Proof of Henselization preserves Milnor squares
nodes.statement: Since $S^h$ is flat over $S$, we can base-change \eqref{milnsquare} along $S \to S^h$ to obtain a new Milnor square \[ \xymatrix{ S^h \ar[d] \ar[r] & T \otimes_S S^h \ar[d] \\ S' \otimes_S S^h \ar[r] & T' \otimes_S S^h }. \] Note that $S' \otimes_S S^h \simeq S'$ by the properties of the henselization, and similarly for $T$. Therefore the bottom arrow can be rewritten as $S' \to T'$. Since this is a Milnor square and the left vertical arrow is a henselian pair, so is the right vertical arrow thanks to Proposition~\ref{checkhensnonunital}. We have a factorization $T \to T \otimes_S S^h \to T'$ as the composite of an ind-\'etale map and a map having the right lifting property with respect to \'etale maps. Thus, the result follows in view of Remark~\ref{hensfact}.
nodes.statement_short: Base-change the Milnor square along the flat map $S\to S^h$ and recognize the henselization via ind-\'etale plus lifting property.

nodes.name: Base change of the square
nodes.statement: Since $S^h$ is flat over $S$, we can base-change \eqref{milnsquare} along $S \to S^h$ to obtain a new Milnor square \[ \xymatrix{ S^h \ar[d] \ar[r] & T \otimes_S S^h \ar[d] \\ S' \otimes_S S^h \ar[r] & T' \otimes_S S^h }. \]
nodes.statement_short: Flat base change gives a new Milnor square.

nodes.name: Identify bottom row
nodes.statement: Note that $S' \otimes_S S^h \simeq S'$ by the properties of the henselization, and similarly for $T$. Therefore the bottom arrow can be rewritten as $S' \to T'$.
nodes.statement_short: Henselization does not change the quotients.

nodes.name: Right arrow henselian
nodes.statement: Since this is a Milnor square and the left vertical arrow is a henselian pair, so is the right vertical arrow thanks to Proposition~\ref{checkhensnonunital}.
nodes.statement_short: Gabber's nonunital criterion.

nodes.name: Recognize henselization
nodes.statement: We have a factorization $T \to T \otimes_S S^h \to T'$ as the composite of an ind-\'etale map and a map having the right lifting property with respect to \'etale maps. Thus, the result follows in view of Remark~\ref{hensfact}.
nodes.statement_short: Ind-\'etale plus lifting property identifies $T^h$.

nodes.name: Nonunital henselization is independent of the base ring
nodes.statement: Let $(S, I)$ be a pair and let $(S^h, I^h)$ be its henselization. Let $R$ be any ring mapping to $S$. Then $I^h$ is the henselization of $I$ as an object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. In particular, the henselization of $I$ as an object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ does not depend on the base ring $R$.
assumptions: $(S, I)$ be a pair and let $(S^h, I^h)$ be its henselization
conclusions: $I^h$ is the henselization of $I$ as an object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$
the henselization of $I$ as an object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ does not depend on the base ring $R$
nodes.label: corollary_hens_ind_of_base

nodes.name: Proof of Nonunital henselization is independent of the base ring
nodes.statement: To distinguish the possible henselizations which a priori might not coincide, we temporarily write $I^{nuh}$ to denote the henselization of $I$ as an object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. The equivalence between $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ and augmented $R$-algebras easily implies that $(R\ltimes I^{nuh},I^{nuh})$ is the henselization of the pair $(R \ltimes I, I)$. Applying Proposition~\ref{milnsquarehens} to the Milnor square \[ \xymatrix{ R\ltimes I \ar[d] \ar[r] & S \ar[d] \\ R \ar[r] & S/I }\] then reveals that the square \[ \xymatrix{ R\ltimes I^{nuh} \ar[d] \ar[r] & S^h \ar[d] \\ R \ar[r] & S^h/I^h }\] is also Milnor, i.e., that $I^{nuh}\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} I^h$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Compare henselizations through the Milnor square relating $R\ltimes I$ and $S$.

nodes.name: Notation $I^{nuh}$ and henselization of $(R\ltimes I,I)$
nodes.statement: To distinguish the possible henselizations which a priori might not coincide, we temporarily write $I^{nuh}$ to denote the henselization of $I$ as an object of $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$. The equivalence between $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R$ and augmented $R$-algebras easily implies that $(R\ltimes I^{nuh},I^{nuh})$ is the henselization of the pair $(R \ltimes I, I)$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $I^{nuh}$; augmented algebras identify $R\ltimes I^{nuh}$ with the henselization.

nodes.name: Milnor square comparison
nodes.statement: Applying Proposition~\ref{milnsquarehens} to the Milnor square \[ \xymatrix{ R\ltimes I \ar[d] \ar[r] & S \ar[d] \\ R \ar[r] & S/I }\] then reveals that the square \[ \xymatrix{ R\ltimes I^{nuh} \ar[d] \ar[r] & S^h \ar[d] \\ R \ar[r] & S^h/I^h }\] is also Milnor, i.e., that $I^{nuh}\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} I^h$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: The henselized Milnor square identifies $I^{nuh}$ with $I^h$.

nodes.name: Endomorphism $[N]$ of free henselian nonunital algebras
nodes.statement: For each $N>0$, denote by \[[N]: \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+\] the endomorphism in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_{\mathbb Z}$ which sends $x_i \mapsto Nx_i$.

nodes.name: Free henselian nonunital $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras as colimits
nodes.statement: Let $n > 0$. The filtered colimit of the endomorphisms $[N]$ on $\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$, indexed over natural numbers $N$ ordered by divisibility, is $\mathbb{Q}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$.
conclusions: The filtered colimit of the endomorphisms $[N]$ on $\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$, indexed over natural numbers $N$ ordered by divisibility, is $\mathbb{Q}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$
nodes.label: rationalhens

nodes.name: Proof of Free henselian nonunital $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras as colimits
nodes.statement: Henselization commutes with filtered colimits, and the filtered colimit of the analogous maps $[N]: \mathbb{Z}[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+$ is given by $\mathbb{Q}[x_1, \dots, x_n]^+$. We now use Corollary \ref{corollary_hens_ind_of_base} that henselization does not depend on the base ring.
nodes.statement_short: Henselization commutes with filtered colimits and is independent of base ring.
nodes.label: sec:kanext

nodes.name: Finitely generated functor
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a small category and $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ a functor. We say that $F$ is \emph{finitely generated} if there exist finitely many objects $X_1, \dots, X_n \in \mathcal{C}$ and a surjection of functors \begin{equation} \bigoplus_{i=1}^t \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, \cdot)] \twoheadrightarrow F. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Surjection from corepresentables
nodes.statement: \bigoplus_{i=1}^t \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_i, \cdot)] \twoheadrightarrow F.
nodes.label: fingenfun

nodes.name: Perfect and pseudocoherent functors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a small category and $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ a functor. \begin{enumerate} \item We say that $F$ is \emph{perfect} if $F$ belongs to the thick subcategory of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathrm{Sp})$ generated by the functors $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, \cdot)$ for $C \in \mathcal{C}$ (or equivalently is a compact object of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$, by a thick subcategory argument). \item We say that $F$ is \emph{pseudocoherent} if, for each $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, there exists a perfect functor $F'$ and a map $F' \to F$ such that $\tau_{\le n}F'(C)\to\tau_{\le n}F(C)$ is an equivalence for all $C\in \mathcal C$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Perfect: in the thick subcategory generated by corepresentables; pseudocoherent: approximated by perfect functors in every truncation range.

nodes.name: Characterizations of pseudocoherence
nodes.statement: Let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$. The following conditions on a functor $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}) \subset \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is pseudocoherent. \item For each $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, the functor $\tau_{\leq n} F$ is a compact object of the $\infty$-category $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$. \item There exists a sequence $G_{d-1} = 0 \to G_d \to G_{d+1} \to G_{d+2} \to \dots $ such that $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is a finite direct sum of functors of the form $\Sigma^i \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, \cdot)$ for $C \in \mathcal{C}$ and such that $\varinjlim_i G_i \simeq F$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Pseudocoherence of a bounded-below functor is equivalent to compactness of truncations and to a cell filtration by corepresentables.
conclusions: The following conditions on a functor $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}) \subset \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ are equivalent
equivalent_conditions: For each $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, the functor $\tau_{\leq n} F$ is a compact object of the $\infty$-category $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$.

There exists a sequence $G_{d-1} = 0 \to G_d \to G_{d+1} \to G_{d+2} \to \dots $ such that $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is a finite direct sum of functors of the form $\Sigma^i \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, \cdot)$ for $C \in \mathcal{C}$ and such that $\varinjlim_i G_i \simeq F$.
nodes.label: pscohcompact

nodes.name: Proof of Characterizations of pseudocoherence
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we can assume $d =0 $ by shifting. For (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2), suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ (we do not need $F$ connective) is pseudocoherent and let $n\in\mathbb Z$. Then by definition there is a perfect functor $F'$ and a map $F' \to F$ inducing an equivalence $\tau_{\leq n} F' \simeq \tau_{\leq n} F$. Since $\tau_{\leq n}: \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}) \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ preserves compact objects (as its right adjoint preserves filtered colimits), it follows that $\tau_{\leq n} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact. For (2) $\Rightarrow$ (3), suppose that $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0})$ and $\tau_{\leq n} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact for each $n$. Then, by assumption $\tau_{\leq 0} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Ab}) \subset \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq 0})$ is a compact object and thus $\pi_0 F$ is a finitely generated functor. We can thus find a functor $G \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0})$ which is a direct sum of $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \cdot)$, for finitely many $X\in\mathcal C$, and a map $G \to F$ which is a surjection on $\pi_0$. Let $F_1 $ be the resulting cofiber and observe that $F_1$ has the same property as $F$ (namely $\tau_{\leq n} F_1 \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact for each $n$, since compact objects are closed under pushouts) and that $F_1 $ is connected. Continuing in this way, we find a sequence of functors $F \to F_1 \to F_2 \to \dots $ such that $F_n$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq n$ and such that the cofiber of each $F_n \to F_{n+1}$ is a finite direct sum of shifts of representables. We obtain the desired sequence $G_n$ by setting $G_n=\operatorname{Fib}(F\to F_{n+1})$. For (3) $\Rightarrow$ (1), note that each $G_n$ is perfect by induction on $n$, and that $G_{n+1}\rightarrow F$ is an equivalence on $\tau_{\leq n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the cycle of implications (1)$\Rightarrow$(2)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(1) by truncation, cell attachment and induction.

nodes.name: Normalize $d=0$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we can assume $d =0 $ by shifting.
nodes.statement_short: Shift to $d=0$.

nodes.name: (1)$\Rightarrow$(2)
nodes.statement: For (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2), suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ (we do not need $F$ connective) is pseudocoherent and let $n\in\mathbb Z$. Then by definition there is a perfect functor $F'$ and a map $F' \to F$ inducing an equivalence $\tau_{\leq n} F' \simeq \tau_{\leq n} F$. Since $\tau_{\leq n}: \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}) \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ preserves compact objects (as its right adjoint preserves filtered colimits), it follows that $\tau_{\leq n} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact.
nodes.statement_short: Truncation preserves compact objects.

nodes.name: (2)$\Rightarrow$(3)
nodes.statement: For (2) $\Rightarrow$ (3), suppose that $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0})$ and $\tau_{\leq n} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact for each $n$. Then, by assumption $\tau_{\leq 0} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Ab}) \subset \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq 0})$ is a compact object and thus $\pi_0 F$ is a finitely generated functor. We can thus find a functor $G \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0})$ which is a direct sum of $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \cdot)$, for finitely many $X\in\mathcal C$, and a map $G \to F$ which is a surjection on $\pi_0$. Let $F_1 $ be the resulting cofiber and observe that $F_1$ has the same property as $F$ (namely $\tau_{\leq n} F_1 \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact for each $n$, since compact objects are closed under pushouts) and that $F_1 $ is connected. Continuing in this way, we find a sequence of functors $F \to F_1 \to F_2 \to \dots $ such that $F_n$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq n$ and such that the cofiber of each $F_n \to F_{n+1}$ is a finite direct sum of shifts of representables. We obtain the desired sequence $G_n$ by setting $G_n=\operatorname{Fib}(F\to F_{n+1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Attach finitely many representable cells inductively.

nodes.name: (3)$\Rightarrow$(1)
nodes.statement: For (3) $\Rightarrow$ (1), note that each $G_n$ is perfect by induction on $n$, and that $G_{n+1}\rightarrow F$ is an equivalence on $\tau_{\leq n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Finite stages are perfect and approximate $F$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{D}$-perfect, $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent and $\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated functors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small full subcategory of a (possibly large, but locally small) category $\mathcal{C}$. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a functor. \begin{enumerate} \item We say that $F$ is \emph{$\mathcal{D}$-perfect} if $F$ belongs to the thick subcategory of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathrm{Sp})$ generated by the functors $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$. \item We say that a functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is called \emph{$\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent} if for each $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, there exists a $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functor $F'$ and a map $F' \to F$ such that $\tau_{\leq n} F'(C) \to \tau_{\leq n} F(C)$ is an equivalence for all $C \in \mathcal{C}$. \item A functor $F_0: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is called \emph{$\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated} if there is a surjection as in \eqref{fingenfun} with $X_i \in \mathcal{D}$ for each $i$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Left Kan extension
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a full subcategory. Given a functor $G: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$, we can form the \emph{left Kan extension} $\mathrm{Lan}(G):\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ (cf. \cite[Sec.~4.3]{HTT}). By definition, for $C \in \mathcal{C}$, $\mathrm{Lan}(G)(C)$ is the colimit $$ \mathrm{Lan}(G)(C) = \varinjlim_{D \to C, D \in \mathcal{D}} G(D) \in \mathrm{Sp}.$$ The construction $F \mapsto \mathrm{Lan}(F)$ is the left adjoint of the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}) \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{D}, \mathrm{Sp})$. A functor $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is said to be \emph{left Kan extended} from $\mathcal{D}$ if the natural map $\mathrm{Lan}( F|_{\mathcal{D}}) \to F$ is an equivalence in $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$. The objects of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ which are left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ form a subcategory equivalent to $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{D}, \mathrm{Sp})$ (via restriction).

nodes.name: $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherence via left Kan extension
nodes.statement: A functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent if and only if it is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent.
conclusions: A functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent if and only if it is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent
equivalent_conditions: it is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent
nodes.label: lkanpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherence via left Kan extension
nodes.statement: The functor $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot) \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$ is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$, so a thick subcategory argument shows that any $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functor is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$. To get the same for any $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functor, note that the truncations $\mathrm{Sp}\rightarrow \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n}$ are a conservative family of colimit-preserving functors, so a functor to $\mathrm{Sp}$ is left Kan extended if and only if its image in each $\mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n}$ is. Conversely, suppose that $F$ is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent. Then $\tau_{\leq n}F\mid_\mathcal{D}\simeq \tau_{\leq n}G\mid_\mathcal{D}$ for some $G:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}$ in the thick subcategory generated by the $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$, and we deduce $\tau_{\leq n}F\simeq \tau_{\leq n}G$ by left Kan extension.
nodes.statement_short: Thick-subcategory argument and truncation for one direction; left Kan extension of approximations for the converse.

nodes.name: Pseudocoherent implies Kan extended
nodes.statement: The functor $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot) \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$ is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$, so a thick subcategory argument shows that any $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functor is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$. To get the same for any $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functor, note that the truncations $\mathrm{Sp}\rightarrow \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n}$ are a conservative family of colimit-preserving functors, so a functor to $\mathrm{Sp}$ is left Kan extended if and only if its image in each $\mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n}$ is.
nodes.statement_short: Thick subcategory and truncation arguments.

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that $F$ is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent. Then $\tau_{\leq n}F\mid_\mathcal{D}\simeq \tau_{\leq n}G\mid_\mathcal{D}$ for some $G:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}$ in the thick subcategory generated by the $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$, and we deduce $\tau_{\leq n}F\simeq \tau_{\leq n}G$ by left Kan extension.
nodes.statement_short: Left Kan extend the approximations from $\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: Filtration criterion for $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherence
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small full subcategory. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$ be a functor for some $d \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item There exists a sequence $G_{d-1} = 0 \to G_d \to G_{d+1} \to G_{d+2} \to \dots $ such that $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is a finite direct sum of functors of the form $\Sigma^i \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$ and such that $\varinjlim_i G_i \simeq F$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$ be a functor for some $d \in \mathbb{Z}$
conclusions: the following are equivalent
equivalent_conditions: There exists a sequence $G_{d-1} = 0 \to G_d \to G_{d+1} \to G_{d+2} \to \dots $ such that $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is a finite direct sum of functors of the form $\Sigma^i \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$ and such that $\varinjlim_i G_i \simeq F$.
nodes.label: pscohfilt2

nodes.name: Proof of Filtration criterion for $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherence
nodes.statement: Combine Lemmas~\ref{lkanpscoh} and \ref{pscohcompact}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two lemmas.

nodes.name: Closure properties of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ a small full subcategory. \begin{enumerate} \item The subcategory of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ spanned by the $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors is thick. \item Let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $K$ be a simplicial set, and let $f: K \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d})$ be a $K$-indexed diagram of functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$. Suppose that the $n$-skeleton $\mathrm{sk}_n K$ is a finite simplicial set for every $n\in\mathbb Z$ and that for each vertex $k_0 \in K_0$, the functor $f(k_0) \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Then the functor $\varinjlim_K f \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item Let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, and let $F_\bullet:\Delta^\sub{op}\to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d})$ be a simplicial object in the category of functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$. Suppose that $F_i$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent for every $i \geq 0$. Then the geometric realization $|F_\bullet|: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item Let $d\in \mathbb Z$, and let $F\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ be a $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functor such that $\pi_nF=0$ for all $n<d$. Then $\pi_d F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is a $\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated functor. \item If $\mathcal{C}$ has finite coproducts and $\mathcal{D}$ is closed under them, then the subcategory of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors in $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is closed under smash products. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors are thick, closed under skeletally finite colimits, geometric realizations and smash products; bottom homotopy is finitely generated.
assumptions: $\mathcal C$ be a category and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ a small full subcategory
conclusions: The subcategory of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ spanned by the $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors is thick.
Then the functor $\varinjlim_K f \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent.
Then the geometric realization $|F_\bullet|: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent.
Then $\pi_d F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is a $\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated functor.
the subcategory of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors in $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is closed under smash products
nodes.label: general:pscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Closure properties of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors
nodes.statement: Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lkanpscoh}, we may assume without loss of generality that $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{D}$, since the property of being left Kan extended is preserved under all colimits. We may also take $d = 0$. Claim (1) follows from Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact} because compact objects (of any $\infty$-category) are closed under finite colimits and retracts. For (2), it suffices by Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact} to show that $\tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_K f )$ is compact as an object of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ for each $n$. But $\tau_{\leq n} f = \tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_{\mathrm{sk}^{n+1} K } f)$ and $\varinjlim_{\mathrm{sk}^{n+1} K } f$ is a finite colimit of pseudocoherent functors, hence pseudocoherent itself by (1); this implies the desired compactness assertion. Claim (3) is handled similarly, because $\tau_{\leq n} ( |F_\bullet|) \simeq \tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_{\Delta_{\leq n+1} }F)$ can be computed as a truncated geometric realization, and this is a finite colimit, cf.~\cite[Lemma~1.2.4.17]{HA}. Claim (4) follows from the filtration Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact}. For (5), it suffices to observe that the smash products of functors of the form $\{\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \cdot)\}_{X \in \mathcal{D}}$ are still of this form under the assumption that $\mathcal{C}$ has finite coproducts and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ is closed under them. It then follows by a thick subcategory argument that the subcategory of $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functors is closed under smash products, which implies the analogous assertion for $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}$ and use compactness of truncations for each closure property.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}$
nodes.statement: Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lkanpscoh}, we may assume without loss of generality that $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{D}$, since the property of being left Kan extended is preserved under all colimits. We may also take $d = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Kan extension reduces to the absolute case with $d=0$.

nodes.name: Claim (1)
nodes.statement: Claim (1) follows from Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact} because compact objects (of any $\infty$-category) are closed under finite colimits and retracts.
nodes.statement_short: Compact objects are closed under finite colimits and retracts.

nodes.name: Claim (2)
nodes.statement: For (2), it suffices by Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact} to show that $\tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_K f )$ is compact as an object of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ for each $n$. But $\tau_{\leq n} f = \tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_{\mathrm{sk}^{n+1} K } f)$ and $\varinjlim_{\mathrm{sk}^{n+1} K } f$ is a finite colimit of pseudocoherent functors, hence pseudocoherent itself by (1); this implies the desired compactness assertion.
nodes.statement_short: Truncations only see a finite skeleton.

nodes.name: Claim (3)
nodes.statement: Claim (3) is handled similarly, because $\tau_{\leq n} ( |F_\bullet|) \simeq \tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_{\Delta_{\leq n+1} }F)$ can be computed as a truncated geometric realization, and this is a finite colimit, cf.~\cite[Lemma~1.2.4.17]{HA}.
nodes.statement_short: Truncated geometric realization is a finite colimit.

nodes.name: Claim (4)
nodes.statement: Claim (4) follows from the filtration Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the filtration characterization.

nodes.name: Claim (5)
nodes.statement: For (5), it suffices to observe that the smash products of functors of the form $\{\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \cdot)\}_{X \in \mathcal{D}}$ are still of this form under the assumption that $\mathcal{C}$ has finite coproducts and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ is closed under them. nodes.statement_short: Smash products of corepresentables are corepresentable.

nodes.name: Goodwillie tower of $\Sigma^\infty\Omega^\infty$
nodes.statement: There is a natural tower $\left\{P_n=P_n ( \Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)\right\}_{n \geq 0}$ of functors $\mathrm{Sp} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ receiving a map from $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty$, \[ \Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty X \to \{ \dots \to P_n (X) \to P_{n-1}(X) \to \dots \to P_1(X) \} \] such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $P_1(X) \simeq X$ and the fiber of $P_n (X) \to P_{n-1} (X) $ is naturally equivalent to $(X^{\otimes n})_{h \Sigma_n}$. \item If $X \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$, the map $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty X \to \varprojlim_n P_n (X)$ is an equivalence and the connectivity of $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty X \to P_n(X)$ tends to $\infty$ with $n$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The Goodwillie tower of $\Sigma^\infty\Omega^\infty$ has layers $(X^{\otimes n})_{h\Sigma_n}$ and converges on connected spectra.
conclusions: There is a natural tower $\left\{P_n=P_n ( \Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)\right\}_{n \geq 0}$ of functors $\mathrm{Sp} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ receiving a map from $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty$
nodes.label: goodwilliefilt

nodes.name: Pseudocoherence and $\Sigma^\infty\Omega^\infty$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category with finite coproducts and let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory closed under finite coproducts. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$ a functor. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item $\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\mathcal{C}$ be a category with finite coproducts
$\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory closed under finite coproducts
conclusions: the following are equivalent
nodes.label: suspensionpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Pseudocoherence and $\Sigma^\infty\Omega^\infty$
nodes.statement: The equivalence of (2) and (3) follows because $\Sigma^\infty, \Sigma^\infty_+$ differ by the constant functor at $S^0$, which is corepresentable since $\mathcal{C}$ has an initial object in $\mathcal{D}$. Suppose $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Using Proposition~\ref{goodwilliefilt}, we conclude that $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is the homotopy limit of a tower whose associated graded is given by $F, (F^{\otimes 2})_{h \Sigma_2}, (F^{\otimes 3})_{h \Sigma_3 }, \dots $. Since $F$ takes values in $\mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$, the connectivity of the associated graded terms tends to $\infty$, so this tower stabilizes in any given finite range. As $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, so are all the graded terms in view of Proposition~\ref{general:pscoh}. It follows that $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Conversely, suppose $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. First, recall that the adjunction $(\Sigma^\infty, \Omega^\infty)$ between the $\infty$-categories of pointed spaces and connective spectra is monadic since $\Omega^\infty|_{\mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0}}$ commutes with sifted colimits \cite[Prop.~1.4.3.9]{HA} and in view of the $\infty$-categorical monadicity theorem \cite[Sec.~4.7.3]{HA}; alternatively, this follows explicitly from delooping machinery going back to \cite{Maygeom}. As a result of monadicity, for any $X \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0}$, one has a natural simplicial spectrum (the bar resolution) $(\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)^{\bullet + 1} X$ whose geometric realization is equivalent to $X$. Therefore, in our case, we can resolve $F$ via the iterates $(\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)^k F$ for $k \geq 1$. By the previous direction and our assumption, each of these is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Thus we have written $F$ as a geometric realization of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$, so $F$ itself is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent.
nodes.statement_short: Goodwillie tower for one direction; bar resolution via monadicity of $\Sigma^\infty\Omega^\infty$ for the converse.

nodes.name: (2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3)

nodes.statement_short: $\Sigma^\infty$ and $\Sigma^\infty_+$ differ by a corepresentable constant.

nodes.name: Terms pseudocoherent

nodes.statement_short: Each iterate is pseudocoherent.

nodes.name: Geometric realization

nodes.statement_short: Geometric realizations preserve pseudocoherence.

nodes.name: Pseudocoherence can be tested after smashing with $H\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a functor. If $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, then $H\mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Conversely, if $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is uniformly bounded-below and $H \mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, so is $F$.
assumptions: $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is uniformly bounded-below and $H \mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent
conclusions: $H\mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent
so is $F$
$H\mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent

nodes.name: Proof of Pseudocoherence can be tested after smashing with $H\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: The first direction follows because we can approximate $H \mathbb{Z}$ in any range by a finite spectrum. The second direction follows because a thick subcategory argument now implies that if $H \mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, so is $\tau_{\leq n} S^0 \otimes F$ for each $n$, and we can approximate $F$ in any given range by $\tau_{\leq n} S^0 \otimes F$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $H\mathbb{Z}$ by finite spectra in a range, and conversely use a thick subcategory argument.

nodes.name: Compact projective henselian nonunital algebras $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$
nodes.statement: We will use the notion of pseudocoherence in the case where $\mathcal{C} = \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ and $\mathcal{D} = (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$ is the category of compact projective objects obtained by idempotent completing the subcategory $\{R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+: n \geq 0\}$ of $ \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$.

nodes.name: Projectively finitely generated and projectively pseudocoherent functors
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item A functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is \emph{projectively finitely generated} if it is $\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated for $\mathcal{D} = (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$. \item A functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is \emph{projectively pseudocoherent} if it is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent for $\mathcal{D} = (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Corepresentables $I\mapsto\Sigma^\infty_+I^n$ are projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: For each $n$, the functor $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ (where $I^n$ here denotes the cartesian product of $n$ copies of $I$) is projectively pseudocoherent. Indeed, it is the suspension spectrum of the corepresentable associated to $ R\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}^+ \in (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$.
nodes.label: ex:pseudocoh

nodes.name: Projectively pseudocoherent functors commute with filtered colimits
nodes.statement: A projectively pseudocoherent functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ commutes with filtered colimits. In fact, the corepresentable functors $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ clearly do, and the result for arbitrary projectively pseudocoherent functors follows because the class of functors $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ which commute with filtered colimits is stable under all colimits. See also Corollary~\ref{kanextcrit} below.
nodes.label: Moved this around and rephrased language slightly

nodes.name: Gabber's lemma on projectively finitely generated functors
nodes.statement: Let $F_0: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ be a projectively finitely generated functor. Suppose that: \begin{enumerate} \item $F_0(I) = 0$ if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is annihilated by an integer $N > 0$. \item $F_0(I) = 0$ if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is a nonunital $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra. \item Given a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the sequence $F_0(I') \to F_0(I) \to F_0(\overline{I}) \to 0$ of abelian groups is exact. \item $F_0$ commutes with filtered colimits. \end{enumerate} Then $F_0 = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: A projectively finitely generated functor vanishing on bounded-torsion and rational henselian algebras, right exact and finitary, is zero.
assumptions: $F_0: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ be a projectively finitely generated functor
$F_0(I) = 0$ if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is annihilated by an integer $N > 0$.
Given a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the sequence $F_0(I') \to F_0(I) \to F_0(\overline{I}) \to 0$ of abelian groups is exact.
nodes.label: gabberlem

nodes.name: Proof of Gabber's lemma on projectively finitely generated functors
nodes.statement: We will prove the following claim: there exists $N\ge1$ such that, for any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the inclusion map $i_N:NI\to I$ induces the zero map $0=(i_N)_*: F_0(NI) \to F_0(I)$. Once this is done, the statement of the lemma will follow by applying (1) and (3) to the short exact sequence $NI\to I\to I/NI$. As in Corollary~\ref{rationalhens}, let $[N]: \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$ be the operator that multiplies each $x_i$ by $N$, so that the colimit of the $[N]$, indexed over $N\ge1$ ordered by divisibility, is $\mathbb{Q}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$. By assumption $F_0$ commutes with filtered colimits and annihilates any nonunital henselian $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra; so, given any element $u \in F_0(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+)$, it follows that there exists $N > 0$ such that $[N]_*(u) = 0$. Now we use that $F_0$ is projectively finitely generated. This means that there exists a surjection \[ \bigoplus_{i=1}^t \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, \cdot)] \to F_0\] of functors for some $n_1,\dots,n_t\ge1$. For each $i=1,\dots,t$, let $g_i\in F_0(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$ be the image of $\mathrm{id}\in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$. Then the above surjection concretely means the following: given any $I\in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ and any element $y\in F_0(I)$, then $y$ is a finite sum of elements of $F_0(I)$ obtained by pushing forward the $g_i$ along various maps $\phi:\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+ \to I$. By the second paragraph, there exists an integer $N > 0$ such that $[N]_*(g_i)=0$ for all the generators $g_i$. From this we can easily complete the proof of the claim, as follows. Given any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, every map $\phi: \mathbb{Z}\{ x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\}^+ \to N I $ has the property that the composite $i_N \circ \phi: \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+ \to I$ factors through $[N]$, i.e., one has a commutative diagram in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ \[ \xymatrix{ \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \ar[r]_-{\phi}\ar[d]^{[N]} & NI \ar[d]^{i_N} \\ \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \ar[r] & I }.\] By choice of $N$ it follows that the composite \[ \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}( \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, NI)] \to F_0(NI) \to F_0(I) \] is zero. But we have shown that every element of $F_0(NI)$ is a finite sum of elements of the form $\phi_*(g_i)$ for various maps $\phi$. Since $g_i \in F_0( \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$ is annihilated by $[N]$, it follows that $(i_N)_*: F_0(NI) \to F_0(I)$ is zero, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Show the inclusion $NI\to I$ induces zero on $F_0$ for some $N$, using finitely many generators killed by $[N]$. The key step is that maps into $NI$ factor through $[N]$ on free algebras.

nodes.name: Reduce to multiplication by $N$
nodes.statement: We will prove the following claim: there exists $N\ge1$ such that, for any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the inclusion map $i_N:NI\to I$ induces the zero map $0=(i_N)_*: F_0(NI) \to F_0(I)$. nodes.statement: Given any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, every map $\phi: \mathbb{Z}\{ x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\}^+ \to N I $ has the property that the composite $i_N \circ \phi: \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+ \to I$ factors through $[N]$, i.e., one has a commutative diagram in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ \[ \xymatrix{ \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \ar[r]_-{\phi}\ar[d]^{[N]} & NI \ar[d]^{i_N} \\ \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \ar[r] & I }.\] By choice of $N$ it follows that the composite \[ \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}( \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, NI)] \to F_0(NI) \to F_0(I) \] is zero.

nodes.name: Vanishing
nodes.statement: But we have shown that every element of $F_0(NI)$ is a finite sum of elements of the form $\phi_*(g_i)$ for various maps $\phi$. Since $g_i \in F_0( \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$ is annihilated by $[N]$, it follows that $(i_N)_*: F_0(NI) \to F_0(I)$ is zero, as claimed.
