nodes.name: Axiomatic rigidity argument
nodes.statement: Let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a projectively pseudocoherent functor. Suppose that: \begin{enumerate} \item For each prime field $R$ and each $n$, we have $F( R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+) = 0$. \item Given a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the sequence $F(I') \to F(I) \to F(\overline{I})$ is a fiber sequence of spectra. \item If $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is nilpotent, then $F(I) = 0$. \end{enumerate} Then $F = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: A projectively pseudocoherent functor on henselian nonunital rings, vanishing on free ones over prime fields and on nilpotents and exact, is zero.
assumptions: For each prime field $R$ and each $n$, we have $F( R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+) = 0$.
Given a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the sequence $F(I') \to F(I) \to F(\overline{I})$ is a fiber sequence of spectra.
nodes.label: pseudoargument

nodes.name: Proof of Axiomatic rigidity argument
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a prime field and restrict $F$ to $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ to obtain a functor $F_R: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$. We observe first that $F_R$ is projectively pseudocoherent (since the building blocks $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ for projectively pseudocoherent functors $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ are independent of the base ring $R$). In particular, $F_R$ is left Kan extended from the subcategory $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$. By assumption, $F_R$ annihilates $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$, so that $F_R = 0$ on $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. It follows that $F$ annihilates any nonunital henselian algebra over a field. Moreover, if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is such that there exists $N \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with $NI = 0$, it follows that $F(I) = 0$: in fact, since $F$ preserves finite products we reduce to the case where $N = p^r$ for some $r$, and then use the short exact sequence $pI \to I \to I/p I$ where $pI$ is nilpotent. The resulting fiber sequence then shows that $F(I) \simeq F(I/pI) = 0$. Suppose $F$ is not the zero functor. Let $d$ be minimal such that $\pi_d F \neq 0$. Then $\pi_d F$ is a projectively finitely generated functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ which commutes with filtered colimits; furthermore, $\pi_d F$ annihilates any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ which is either of bounded torsion or a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space. Using Lemma~\ref{gabberlem} below, we find that $\pi_d F = 0$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing on free algebras over prime fields gives vanishing over fields and bounded torsion; a minimal nonzero homotopy group contradicts Gabber's lemma.

nodes.name: Vanishing over prime fields
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a prime field and restrict $F$ to $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ to obtain a functor $F_R: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$. We observe first that $F_R$ is projectively pseudocoherent (since the building blocks $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ for projectively pseudocoherent functors $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ are independent of the base ring $R$). In particular, $F_R$ is left Kan extended from the subcategory $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$. By assumption, $F_R$ annihilates $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$, so that $F_R = 0$ on $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$.
nodes.statement_short: Restricted functor is Kan extended from free objects, hence zero.

nodes.name: Bounded torsion
nodes.statement: It follows that $F$ annihilates any nonunital henselian algebra over a field. Moreover, if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is such that there exists $N \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with $NI = 0$, it follows that $F(I) = 0$: in fact, since $F$ preserves finite products we reduce to the case where $N = p^r$ for some $r$, and then use the short exact sequence $pI \to I \to I/p I$ where $pI$ is nilpotent. The resulting fiber sequence then shows that $F(I) \simeq F(I/pI) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Use products and the nilpotent ideal $pI$.

nodes.name: Contradiction via Gabber's lemma
nodes.statement: Suppose $F$ is not the zero functor. Let $d$ be minimal such that $\pi_d F \neq 0$. Then $\pi_d F$ is a projectively finitely generated functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ which commutes with filtered colimits; furthermore, $\pi_d F$ annihilates any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ which is either of bounded torsion or a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space. Using Lemma~\ref{gabberlem} below, we find that $\pi_d F = 0$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Bottom homotopy group violates Gabber's lemma.

nodes.name: Minimal nonvanishing degree
nodes.statement: Suppose $F$ is not the zero functor. Let $d$ be minimal such that $\pi_d F \neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $d$ minimal with $\pi_dF\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Properties of $\pi_dF$
nodes.statement: Then $\pi_d F$ is a projectively finitely generated functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ which commutes with filtered colimits; furthermore, $\pi_d F$ annihilates any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ which is either of bounded torsion or a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space.
nodes.statement_short: It is projectively finitely generated, finitary, vanishing on torsion and rational algebras.

nodes.name: Apply Gabber's lemma
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{gabberlem} below, we find that $\pi_d F = 0$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Gabber's lemma gives $\pi_dF=0$.

nodes.name: Kan extension via simplicial resolutions (condition (Kan))
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category that has sifted colimits, fix a base ring $R$ and a functor \[ F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}, \] and consider the following condition on $F$: \begin{itemize} \item[(Kan)] $F$ is left Kan extended from the subcatgory $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. \end{itemize} Suppose $F$ satisfies (Kan). Then one can compute $F$ from its values on $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$ as follows. First, $F$ commutes with filtered colimits, and hence its value is determined on all free objects in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. Next, if $I$ is an arbitrary nonunital henselian $R$-algebra, then there exists an augmented simplicial object $I_\bullet:\Delta^\sub{op}_+ \to \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ such that $I_{-1} = I$, each $I_i$ is a free algebra in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$, and $|I_\bullet| \simeq I_{-1} = I$, i.e., $I_\bullet$ is a simplicial resolution of $I$ by free objects; then the value of $F$ on $I$ is given by $F(I) = |F(I_\bullet)|$. The construction of such simplicial resolutions (and the independence of choices) is a general homotopical technique going back to Quillen \cite{QuillenHA}, originally developed to build the cotangent complex via simplicial commutative rings. Using the results of \cite{QuillenHA} (which work in particular for any category satisfying (Law) from Remark \ref{remark_Lawvere}, by \cite[Rmk.~1, pg.~II.4.2]{QuillenHA}), we can make the category $\mathrm{Fun}( \Delta^\sub{op}, \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R)$ of simplicial nonunital henselian $R$-algebras into a model category where the weak equivalences and fibrations are those of underlying simplicial sets. The resolution $I_\bullet$ of $I$ is then obtained as a cofibrant replacement in this model category of the constant simplicial object $I$. This can also be phrased using the language of nonabelian derived $\infty$-categories \cite[Sec.~5.5.8]{HTT}. We record these observations for the future in the following corollary which does not mention simplicial non-unital henselian rings. \begin{corollary} Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category with sifted colimits, and let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}$ be a functor. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is left Kan extended from $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma} \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. \item Whenever $I_\bullet$ is a simplicial object in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ whose geometric realization is equivalent to $I_{-1} \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ (in particular, the homotopy type of the underlying simplicial set of $I_\bullet$ is discrete), then the map $|F(I_\bullet)| \to F(I_{-1})$ is an equivalence.\footnote{Since the category of nonunital henselian rings is the category of algebras over a monad on the category of sets, there is always a canonical resolution of any object by free objects; it would suffice to consider these resolutions.} Furthermore, $F$ commutes with filtered colimits. \end{enumerate} \end{corollary}
nodes.statement_short: Functors left Kan extended from compact projectives are computed by simplicial resolutions by free henselian nonunital algebras.
nodes.label: kanextsifted

nodes.name: Criterion for left Kan extension from compact projectives
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category with sifted colimits, and let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}$ be a functor. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is left Kan extended from $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma} \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. \item Whenever $I_\bullet$ is a simplicial object in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ whose geometric realization is equivalent to $I_{-1} \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ (in particular, the homotopy type of the underlying simplicial set of $I_\bullet$ is discrete), then the map $|F(I_\bullet)| \to F(I_{-1})$ is an equivalence.\footnote{Since the category of nonunital henselian rings is the category of algebras over a monad on the category of sets, there is always a canonical resolution of any object by free objects; it would suffice to consider these resolutions.} Furthermore, $F$ commutes with filtered colimits. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: the following are equivalent
nodes.label: kanextcrit

nodes.name: Singular chains $C_*(X;\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: Given a space $X$, we write $C_*(X; \mathbb{Z}) = H\mathbb{Z}\otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ X$ for the singular chains on $X$ with $\mathbb{Z}$-coefficients, viewed as a (generalized) Eilenberg--MacLane spectrum.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of homology of $BGL_\infty$
nodes.statement: The functor $ \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto C_*( BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
conclusions: The functor $ \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto C_*( BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.label: glpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Projective pseudocoherence of homology of $BGL_\infty$
nodes.statement: First, by the homological stability results of Maazen and van der Kallen \cite{vdK}, we can approximate $C_*(BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ by $C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ in any given finite range. It is crucial for us that this stability range is independent of the choice of $I$: namely, the stability range depends on the Krull dimension of the maximal spectrum of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$, but since $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical this is the maximal spectrum of $\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, it suffices to show that for any $n$, the functor $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent. We use the short exact sequence of groups \[ 1 \to GL_n(1 + I) \to GL_n( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) \to GL_n(\mathbb{Z}) \to 1, \] where $GL_n(1 + I)$ is, by definition, the kernel of the second map in the above sequence. It follows that there is a $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-action on $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ and we have \begin{equation} C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z}) \simeq C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})_{h GL_n(\mathbb{Z})}. \end{equation} We next argue that the functor $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent. Note that as a set, $GL_n(1 + I)$ is naturally isomorphic to the cartesian product $I^{n^2}$ since $I$ is contained in the radical of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$. Now we observe that using the classical bar construction and the isomorphism (of sets) $GL_n(1 + I) \simeq I^{n^2}$, that $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is a geometric realization of functors of the form $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}]$ for $i \geq 0$. Since the functor $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}] \simeq H \mathbb{Z} \otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n^2i}\right\}^+, I)$ is clearly projectively pseudocoherent, it follows that $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 +I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent as desired. Finally, the group $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite index normal subgroup $N \leq GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $BN$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, by the existence of the Borel-Serre compactification (see \cite{Serresurvey} for a survey). Since $(-)_{hGL_n(\mathbb{Z})} \simeq ((-)_{hN})_{h(G/N)}$, we conclude by two applications of Proposition \ref{general:pscoh} that taking $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-homotopy orbits preserves projective pseudocoherence. Therefore, we conclude in view of the previous paragraph and \eqref{glnZorbit}.
nodes.statement_short: Homological stability reduces to $GL_n$; express via $GL_n(1+I)\cong I^{n^2}$ and bar construction, then take $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-orbits using Borel--Serre.

nodes.name: Homological stability
nodes.statement: First, by the homological stability results of Maazen and van der Kallen \cite{vdK}, we can approximate $C_*(BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ by $C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ in any given finite range. It is crucial for us that this stability range is independent of the choice of $I$: namely, the stability range depends on the Krull dimension of the maximal spectrum of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$, but since $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical this is the maximal spectrum of $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $BGL_\infty$ by $BGL_n$ uniformly in $I$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $GL_n$
nodes.statement: Thus, it suffices to show that for any $n$, the functor $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to fixed $n$.

nodes.name: Extension by $GL_n(1+I)$
nodes.statement: We use the short exact sequence of groups \[ 1 \to GL_n(1 + I) \to GL_n( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) \to GL_n(\mathbb{Z}) \to 1, \] where $GL_n(1 + I)$ is, by definition, the kernel of the second map in the above sequence. It follows that there is a $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-action on $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ and we have \begin{equation} C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z}) \simeq C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})_{h GL_n(\mathbb{Z})}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write as homotopy orbits of $GL_n(1+I)$-chains.

nodes.name: Homology of $BGL_n(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I)$ as homotopy orbits
nodes.statement: C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z}) \simeq C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})_{h GL_n(\mathbb{Z})}.
nodes.label: glnZorbit

nodes.name: $GL_n(1+I)$-chains
nodes.statement: We next argue that the functor $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent. Note that as a set, $GL_n(1 + I)$ is naturally isomorphic to the cartesian product $I^{n^2}$ since $I$ is contained in the radical of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$. Now we observe that using the classical bar construction and the isomorphism (of sets) $GL_n(1 + I) \simeq I^{n^2}$, that $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is a geometric realization of functors of the form $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}]$ for $i \geq 0$. Since the functor $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}] \simeq H \mathbb{Z} \otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n^2i}\right\}^+, I)$ is clearly projectively pseudocoherent, it follows that $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 +I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Show $I\mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1+I))$ is projectively pseudocoherent.

nodes.name: $GL_n(1+I)\cong I^{n^2}$
nodes.statement: Note that as a set, $GL_n(1 + I)$ is naturally isomorphic to the cartesian product $I^{n^2}$ since $I$ is contained in the radical of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the group with a product of copies of $I$.

nodes.name: Bar construction
nodes.statement: Now we observe that using the classical bar construction and the isomorphism (of sets) $GL_n(1 + I) \simeq I^{n^2}$, that $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is a geometric realization of functors of the form $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}]$ for $i \geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Geometric realization of functors $\mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2 i}]$.

nodes.name: Corepresentable terms
nodes.statement: Since the functor $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}] \simeq H \mathbb{Z} \otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n^2i}\right\}^+, I)$ is clearly projectively pseudocoherent, it follows that $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 +I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent as desired.
nodes.statement_short: The terms are corepresentable.

nodes.name: Borel--Serre
nodes.statement: Finally, the group $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite index normal subgroup $N \leq GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $BN$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, by the existence of the Borel-Serre compactification (see \cite{Serresurvey} for a survey). Since $(-)_{hGL_n(\mathbb{Z})} \simeq ((-)_{hN})_{h(G/N)}$, we conclude by two applications of Proposition \ref{general:pscoh} that taking $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-homotopy orbits preserves projective pseudocoherence.
nodes.statement_short: Homotopy orbits by $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ preserve projective pseudocoherence.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, we conclude in view of the previous paragraph and \eqref{glnZorbit}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the homotopy orbit formula.

nodes.name: $K_0$ is rigid for henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then $K_0(R) \simeq K_0(R/I)$.
conclusions: $K_0(R) \simeq K_0(R/I)$
nodes.label: K0invhenspair

nodes.name: Proof of $K_0$ is rigid for henselian pairs
nodes.statement: In fact, we claim that isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $R$ modules and isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $R/I$-modules agree. For one direction, if $M, N$ are finitely generated projective $R$-modules, then any isomorphism $M/IM \simeq N/IM$ can be lifted to a map $M \to N$, which is necessarily an isomorphism by Nakayama's lemma applied to the kernel; we use here that $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $R$. For the other direction, by lifting idempotents any projective $R/I$-module lifts to $R$, cf. \cite[Tag 0D49]{stacks-project}.
nodes.statement_short: Lift isomorphisms by Nakayama and projectives by lifting idempotents.

nodes.name: Projectives correspond
nodes.statement: In fact, we claim that isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $R$ modules and isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $R/I$-modules agree.
nodes.statement_short: Isomorphism classes of projectives agree.

nodes.name: Isomorphisms lift
nodes.statement: For one direction, if $M, N$ are finitely generated projective $R$-modules, then any isomorphism $M/IM \simeq N/IM$ can be lifted to a map $M \to N$, which is necessarily an isomorphism by Nakayama's lemma applied to the kernel; we use here that $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Nakayama's lemma.

nodes.name: Projectives lift
nodes.statement: For the other direction, by lifting idempotents any projective $R/I$-module lifts to $R$, cf. \cite[Tag 0D49]{stacks-project}.
nodes.statement_short: Lifting idempotents.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of K-theory
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto K( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
conclusions: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto K( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.label: Kpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Projective pseudocoherence of K-theory
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is henselian, we have $K_0( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) = \mathbb{Z}$ by Lemma \ref{K0invhenspair}; since the constant functor $\mathbb{Z}$ is projectively pseudocoherent, it remains to see that the functor $I \mapsto \tau_{\geq 1} K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent. By Propositions \ref{suspensionpscoh} and \ref{HZpscoh} and the plus-construction description of $K$-theory (cf.~\cite[IV.1]{KBook} for an account), it suffices to check that the functor \[I \mapsto H \mathbb{Z} \otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega^\infty \tau_{\geq 1} K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) \simeq C_*(BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})\] is projectively pseudocoherent, which follows from Proposition~\ref{glpscoh} above.
nodes.statement_short: $K_0$ is constant by rigidity; reduce $\tau_{\geq 1}K$ via plus-construction to homology of $BGL_\infty$.

nodes.name: K-theory of henselian nonunital rings commutes with simplicial resolutions
nodes.statement: In particular, Proposition \ref{Kpscoh} shows that the functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$, $I \mapsto K( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ commutes with simplicial resolutions in view of Construction~\ref{kanextsifted}. The same argument shows that this also holds in the larger category of nonunital local rings, even without the henselian condition. This observation, in various forms, plays an important role in the study of the local structure of $K$-theory. Compare, for instance \cite[Lemma I.2.2]{Goodrel} for the nilpotent case and \cite[Ch.~III, Prop.~1.4.2]{dgm} for a more general assertion for radical pairs.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of the Eilenberg--MacLane functor
nodes.statement: The Eilenberg--MacLane functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto HI$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
conclusions: The Eilenberg--MacLane functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto HI$ is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.label: EMpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of projective pseudocoherence of the Eilenberg--MacLane functor
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{EMpscoh} is a direct consequence of the following result, in the context of abelian groups.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce from the $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherence of $A\mapsto HA$ on abelian groups.

nodes.name: Eilenberg--MacLane functor on abelian groups is $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Ab}$ be the category of abelian groups. The functor $\mathrm{Ab} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $A \mapsto HA$ is $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherent for $\mathrm{Latt} \subset \mathrm{Ab}$ the subcategory of finitely generated free abelian groups.
conclusions: The functor $\mathrm{Ab} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $A \mapsto HA$ is $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherent for $\mathrm{Latt} \subset \mathrm{Ab}$ the subcategory of finitely generated free abelian groups
nodes.label: Abpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Eilenberg--MacLane functor on abelian groups is $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: We can write functorially $HA = \varinjlim_n \Sigma^{-n}\Sigma^\infty K(A, n)$ for $K(A, n)$ the $n$th Eilenberg--MacLane space for $A$. This colimit stabilizes in any ranges of degrees by the Freudenthal suspension theorem, so it suffices to show that the functor $A \mapsto \Sigma^\infty K(A, n)$ is projectively pseudocoherent. But this follows from the iterated bar construction which gives a functorial model for $K(A, n)$ as the colimit of an $n$-fold simplicial space each of whose terms is a product of copies of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $HA$ as a colimit of suspension spectra of Eilenberg--MacLane spaces modeled by iterated bar constructions.

nodes.name: Colimit formula
nodes.statement: We can write functorially $HA = \varinjlim_n \Sigma^{-n}\Sigma^\infty K(A, n)$ for $K(A, n)$ the $n$th Eilenberg--MacLane space for $A$.
nodes.statement_short: $HA=\varinjlim\Sigma^{-n}\Sigma^\infty K(A,n)$.

nodes.name: Freudenthal
nodes.statement: This colimit stabilizes in any ranges of degrees by the Freudenthal suspension theorem, so it suffices to show that the functor $A \mapsto \Sigma^\infty K(A, n)$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.statement_short: Stabilization reduces to $\Sigma^\infty K(A,n)$.

nodes.name: Bar construction
nodes.statement: But this follows from the iterated bar construction which gives a functorial model for $K(A, n)$ as the colimit of an $n$-fold simplicial space each of whose terms is a product of copies of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Products of copies of $A$.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of THH
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto \mathrm{THH}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
conclusions: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto \mathrm{THH}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.label: THHps

nodes.name: Proof of Projective pseudocoherence of THH
nodes.statement: Using the cyclic bar construction for $\mathrm{THH}$, this follows because all the terms $(H(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I))^{\otimes k}$ (of which $\mathrm{THH}$ is a geometric realization) are projectively pseudocoherent in view of Lemma~\ref{EMpscoh} and Proposition~\ref{general:pscoh}.
nodes.statement_short: Cyclic bar construction with terms projectively pseudocoherent.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of TC/p
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto \mathrm{TC}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
conclusions: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto \mathrm{TC}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p$ is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.label: TCpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Projective pseudocoherence of TC/p
nodes.statement: This now follows from Lemma~\ref{THHps} and Proposition~\ref{strong:finiteness}. Indeed, for any of the functors $F$ in the statement of the latter, we have that $I \mapsto F( \mathrm{THH}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I))$ is projectively pseudocoherent (note that taking $S^1$-homotopy orbits preserves pseudocoherence thanks to Lemma~\ref{general:pscoh}, as the skeleta of $BS^1$ are finite complexes), and then we can approximate $\mathrm{TC}/p$ in any range.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate TC/p by homotopy orbit functors applied to THH.

nodes.name: Logarithmic forms $\nu^n$ and $\widetilde{\nu}^n$
nodes.statement: For an $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$, we let $\nu^n(R) = \ker( 1 - C^{-1}: \Omega^n_R \to \Omega^n_R / d \Omega^{n-1}_R)$. We will also write this as $\Omega^n_{R, \mathrm{log}}$. We also let $\widetilde{\nu^n}(R)$ be the cokernel of $1 - C^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\nu^n$ and $\widetilde{\nu}^n$ are the kernel and cokernel of $1-C^{-1}$ on $n$-forms.

nodes.name: Differential forms under \'etale maps
nodes.statement: Let $R \to S$ be an \'etale map of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras. Let $R^{(1)} \rightarrow R, S^{(1)} \rightarrow S$ be the Frobenius twists of $R$ and $S$.\footnote{Thus $R^{(1)}$ consists of formal expressions of the form ``$a^p$", and the map to $R$ is ``$a^p$" $\mapsto a^p$. More straightforwardly, we can set $R^{(1)}=R$ and take the map $R^{(1)}=R\rightarrow R$ to be the Frobenius.} Then: \begin{enumerate} \item The map $\Omega^n_R \otimes_R S \to \Omega^n_S$ is an isomorphism. \item The de Rham differentials $d: \Omega^{n-1}_R \to \Omega^n_R, \Omega^{n-1}_S \to \Omega^n_S$ are respectively $R^{(1)}, S^{(1)}$-linear so that the quotients $\Omega^n_R/d \Omega_R^{n-1} , \Omega^n_S/d \Omega_S^{n-1} $ inherit the structure of $R^{(1)}, S^{(1)}$-modules respectively. The map $\Omega^n_R/d \Omega_R^{n-1} \otimes_{R^{(1)}} S^{(1)} \to \Omega^n_S/d\Omega^{n-1}_S$ is an isomorphism. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The map $\Omega^n_R \otimes_R S \to \Omega^n_S$ is an isomorphism.
The map $\Omega^n_R/d \Omega_R^{n-1} \otimes_{R^{(1)}} S^{(1)} \to \Omega^n_S/d\Omega^{n-1}_S$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: qcohomega

nodes.name: Proof of Differential forms under \'etale maps
nodes.statement: Part (1) is standard. Since $R \to S$ is \'etale, the natural square linking $R^{(1)}, R, S^{(1)}$ and $S$ is cocartesian (cf.~\cite[Tag 0EBS]{stacks-project}), which now implies (2).
nodes.statement_short: (1) is standard; (2) from the cocartesian Frobenius-twist square for \'etale maps.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: Part (1) is standard.
nodes.statement_short: Standard.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: Since $R \to S$ is \'etale, the natural square linking $R^{(1)}, R, S^{(1)}$ and $S$ is cocartesian (cf.~\cite[Tag 0EBS]{stacks-project}), which now implies (2).
nodes.statement_short: Frobenius-twist square is cocartesian.

nodes.name: Geisser--Levine and Geisser--Hesselholt calculations
conclusions: There is a natural map $\pi_n ( K(R)/p) \rightarrow \nu^n(R)$, which is an isomorphism if $R$ is local.
There is a functorial exact sequence $0 \to \widetilde{\nu}^{n+1}(R) \to \pi_n ( \mathrm{TC}(R)/p) \to {\nu}^{n}(R) \to 0$.
If $R$ is local, we have a functorial identification $\pi_n ( K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p) \simeq \widetilde{\nu}^{n+2}(R)$.
nodes.label: GHGL

nodes.statement: In the \'etale topology, there is a short exact sequence of sheaves $0 \to \nu^n \to \Omega^n \xrightarrow{1 - C^{-1}} \Omega^n/d \Omega^{n-1} \to 0$, and the second and third terms are quasi-coherent (either over the structure sheaf or its Frobenius twist by Lemma~\ref{qcohomega}), so have no higher cohomology on affines.

nodes.name: Solving $x - sx^n = 1$ in henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Let $s \in I$ and let $n \geq 1$. Then the equation $x - s x^n = 1$ can be solved in $R$.
conclusions: the equation $x - s x^n = 1$ can be solved in $R$
nodes.label: solveeq:hens

nodes.name: Proof of Solving $x - sx^n = 1$ in henselian pairs
nodes.statement: The equation has a simple root in $R/I$ (namely, $x = 1$), which therefore admits a lift to $R$ by definition of henselian.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the simple root $x=1$ by henselianity.

nodes.name: Rigidity of $\nu^n$ and $\widetilde{\nu}^n$ for henselian pairs
assumptions: $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
conclusions: the map $\nu^n(R) \to \nu^n(R/I)$ is surjective
the map $\widetilde{\nu}^{n}(R) \to \widetilde{\nu}^n(R/I)$ is an isomorphism
nodes.label: toyFprigidityTC

nodes.name: Proof of Rigidity of $\nu^n$ and $\widetilde{\nu}^n$ for henselian pairs
nodes.statement_short: Snake lemma reduces to surjectivity on kernels; solve $u-u^pa^{p-1}x^{p-1}=1$ by henselianity.

nodes.name: Kernels $V_0,V_1$
nodes.statement: We use the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ V_0 \ar[d] \ar[r] & V_1 \ar[d] \\ \Omega^n_R \ar[r]^-{1 - C^{-1}} \ar[d] & \Omega^n_R/ d \Omega^{n-1}_R \ar[d] \\ \Omega^n_{R/I} \ar[r]^-{1 - C^{-1}} & \Omega^n_{R/I}/ d \Omega^{n-1}_{R/I} }\] where we define $V_0, V_1$ to be the kernels of the surjective vertical maps $\Omega^n_R \to \Omega^n_{R/I}$ and $\Omega^n_R/ d \Omega^{n-1}_R \to \Omega^n_{R/I}/ d \Omega^{n-1}_{R/I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Diagram with kernels of reduction.

nodes.name: Reduce to surjectivity
nodes.statement_short: Snake lemma reduction.

nodes.name: Generators of $V_1$
nodes.statement: Consider a differential form $\omega = a dx_1 dx_2 \dots dx_n \in \Omega^n_R$ such that one of $\left\{a, x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ belongs to $I$ (here $n = 0$ is allowed). The image of such a class in $\Omega^n_R/d \Omega_R^{n-1}$ belongs to $V_1$, and $V_1$ is generated by such classes.
nodes.statement_short: Forms with a coefficient in $I$ generate.

nodes.name: Twisted form
nodes.statement: For $u \in R$, we have $$(1 - C^{-1}) ( u \omega) = (u - u^p a^{p-1} x_1^{p-1} \dots x_n^{p-1}) \omega.$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $(1-C^{-1})(u\omega)$.

nodes.name: Solve for $u$
nodes.statement: Since $(R, I)$ is a henselian pair and $a^{p-1} x_1^{p-1} \dots x_n^{p-1}\in I$, we can choose $u \in R$ such that $u - u^p a^{p-1} x_1^{p-1} \dots x_n^{p-1} = 1$, using Lemma~\ref{solveeq:hens}.
nodes.statement_short: Solve $u-u^pa^{p-1}\cdots=1$ by henselianity.

nodes.name: Conclude surjectivity
nodes.statement: The class $u \omega \in \Omega^n_R$ belongs to $V_0$ and has image given by $\omega$; so $\omega$ is in the image of $V_0 \to V_1$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: $u\omega\in V_0$ maps to $\omega$.

nodes.name: Rigidity of $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ for ind-smooth henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
nodes.statement: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be an ind-smooth henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra with residue field $k$. Then the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$.
assumptions: $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be an ind-smooth henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra with residue field $k$
conclusions: the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
nodes.label: rigidity:henspaircharp

nodes.name: Proof of Rigidity of $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ for ind-smooth henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{GHGL}, it suffices to show that the map \( \widetilde{\nu}^n(R) \to \widetilde{\nu}^n(k) \) is an isomorphism. This follows from Proposition~\ref{toyFprigidityTC}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Geisser--Levine/Hesselholt calculation and rigidity of $\widetilde{\nu}^n$.

nodes.name: Nonconnective $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$
nodes.statement: For this, we need to invoke the non-connective variant $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$ of $K^{\operatorname{inv}}$, defined as the fiber of the cyclotomic trace $\mathbb{K}\rightarrow \mathrm{TC}$ from non-connective $K$-theory.

nodes.name: Excision for $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$
nodes.statement: Suppose $R$ is a unital associative ring, $I\subset R$ a two-sided ideal, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ a homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to a two-sided ideal $J$ of $S$ (so one has a Milnor square, cf.~ Definition~\ref{milnorsquare}). Then the induced map $$\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)\rightarrow \mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(S,J)$$ is an equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: Relative $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$ depends only on the ideal (excision).
assumptions: $R$ is a unital associative ring, $I\subset R$ a two-sided ideal, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ a homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to a two-sided ideal $J$ of $S$
conclusions: the induced map $$\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)\rightarrow \mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(S,J)$$ is an equivalence
nodes.label: DKGHC

nodes.name: $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$ of a non-unital ring
nodes.statement: This can be read as saying that $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)$ ``only depends on $I$." To make this precise, one can define $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(I) = \mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I,I)$ for any non-unital ring $I$.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$ is exact on short exact sequences of non-unital rings
nodes.statement: Clearly the new $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$ restricts to the old one on unital rings; moreover, Theorem \ref{DKGHC} implies that $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$ sends short exact sequences $I'\rightarrow I\twoheadrightarrow I''$ of non-unital rings to fiber sequences of spectra.
conclusions: $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$ sends short exact sequences $I'\rightarrow I\twoheadrightarrow I''$ of non-unital rings to fiber sequences of spectra

nodes.name: $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}(I)$ computes relative $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$
nodes.statement: In particular, $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(I) \simeq \mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)$ whenever $I$ embeds as a two-sided ideal in $R$, in view of Theorem~\ref{DKGHC} applied to the map $(\mathbb{Z} \oplus I, I) \to (R, I)$ of pairs of rings with an ideal.
assumptions: $I$ embeds as a two-sided ideal in $R$
conclusions: $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(I) \simeq \mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)$

nodes.name: Connective versus nonconnective relative K-theory of henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Suppose $(R,I)$ is a henselian pair, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J$ of $S$. Then the square of spectra \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ K(R, I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & K(S, J) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{K}(R, I) \ar[r] & \mathbb{K}(S, J) }\end{equation} is cartesian.
assumptions: $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J$ of $S$
conclusions: the square of spectra
is cartesian

nodes.name: Square of relative connective and nonconnective K-theory
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ K(R, I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & K(S, J) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{K}(R, I) \ar[r] & \mathbb{K}(S, J) }
nodes.label: Ksquare

nodes.name: Proof of Connective versus nonconnective relative K-theory of henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the fiber of the top horizontal map and let $\mathbb{F}$ be the fiber of the bottom horizontal map. Note that the maps $K(R) \to \mathbb{K}(R), K(R/I) \to \mathbb{K}(R/I)$, etc.\ are equivalences in degrees $ \geq 0$; thus, taking fibers, the maps $K(R, I) \to \mathbb{K}(R, I)$ and $K(S, J) \to \mathbb{K}(S, J)$ are equivalences in degrees $\geq 0$. Taking fibers again, we find that the map $F \to \mathbb{F}$ is an equivalence in degrees $\geq 0$. On the other hand, $\mathbb{F}$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$ (even $\geq 1$) by the excision theorem of Bass and Bass--Heller--Swan, \cite[Thm.~XII.8.3]{Bass}. Thus it suffices to show that $F$ is also concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$. But since $(R, I)$ and $(S, J)$ are henselian pairs, it follows by Lemma~\ref{K0invhenspair} that the maps $K_0(R) \to K_0(R/I), K_0(S) \to K_0(S/J)$ are isomorphisms and the maps $K_1(R) \to K_1(R/I), K_1(S) \to K_1(S/J)$ (which are the abelianizations of $GL_\infty(R) \to GL_\infty(R/I), GL_\infty(S) \to GL_\infty(S/J)$) are surjections; thus $K(R, I)$ and $K(S, J)$ are concentrated in degrees $\geq 1$, so that $F$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Compare fibers in degrees $\geq 0$; nonconnective fiber is connective by Bass excision and connective fiber by $K_0$, $K_1$ rigidity.

nodes.name: Fibers $F$, $\mathbb{F}$
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the fiber of the top horizontal map and let $\mathbb{F}$ be the fiber of the bottom horizontal map. Note that the maps $K(R) \to \mathbb{K}(R), K(R/I) \to \mathbb{K}(R/I)$, etc.\ are equivalences in degrees $ \geq 0$; thus, taking fibers, the maps $K(R, I) \to \mathbb{K}(R, I)$ and $K(S, J) \to \mathbb{K}(S, J)$ are equivalences in degrees $\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Relative maps are equivalences in nonnegative degrees.

nodes.name: $F\to\mathbb{F}$ in degrees $\geq 0$
nodes.statement: Taking fibers again, we find that the map $F \to \mathbb{F}$ is an equivalence in degrees $\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Fibers agree in nonnegative degrees.

nodes.name: Bass excision
nodes.statement: On the other hand, $\mathbb{F}$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$ (even $\geq 1$) by the excision theorem of Bass and Bass--Heller--Swan, \cite[Thm.~XII.8.3]{Bass}. Thus it suffices to show that $F$ is also concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Nonconnective fiber is connective.

nodes.name: Rigidity of $K_0,K_1$
nodes.statement: But since $(R, I)$ and $(S, J)$ are henselian pairs, it follows by Lemma~\ref{K0invhenspair} that the maps $K_0(R) \to K_0(R/I), K_0(S) \to K_0(S/J)$ are isomorphisms and the maps $K_1(R) \to K_1(R/I), K_1(S) \to K_1(S/J)$ (which are the abelianizations of $GL_\infty(R) \to GL_\infty(R/I), GL_\infty(S) \to GL_\infty(S/J)$) are surjections; thus $K(R, I)$ and $K(S, J)$ are concentrated in degrees $\geq 1$, so that $F$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Relative $K$ is $1$-connective.

nodes.name: Excision for $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ of henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Suppose $(R,I)$ is a henselian pair, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism which restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J\subset S$. Then the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R, I) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(S, J)$ is an equivalence.
assumptions: $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism which restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J\subset S$
conclusions: the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R, I) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(S, J)$ is an equivalence
nodes.label: replaceexcision

nodes.name: Proof of Excision for $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ of henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Combining with the homotopy cartesian square \eqref{Ksquare} between relative connective and nonconnective $K$-theory, we find that the result now follows from Theorem~\ref{DKGHC}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the cartesian square with excision for $\mathbb{K}^{\mathrm{inv}}$.

nodes.name: Main rigidity theorem for $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ of henselian pairs
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then for any prime number $p$, the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$. Equivalently, the map $K(R, I) \to \mathrm{TC}(R, I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: For a henselian pair, $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ mod $p$ is invariant under passing to $R/I$; equivalently relative K-theory and TC agree mod $p$.
conclusions: the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
the map $K(R, I) \to \mathrm{TC}(R, I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
also_stated_at: \label{ourthm} Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then for any $n$, the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/n \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/n$ is an equivalence.
nodes.label: mainthm

nodes.name: Proof of Main rigidity theorem for $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ of henselian pairs
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision}, it suffices to consider the case where $(R, I) = (\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ where $I$ is a nonunital henselian ring. We now consider the functor \[ F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}, \quad F(I) = K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)/p. \] By Propositions~\ref{Kpscoh} and \ref{TCpscoh}, $F$ is a projectively pseudocoherent functor. Implicit here is the statement (due to Quillen) that the $K$-groups of $\mathbb{Z}$ are finitely generated, as are the mod $p$ homotopy groups of $\mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z})$ (both of which follow from evaluating the projectively pseudocoherent functors $I \mapsto K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I), \mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p$ at $I = 0$). The assertion of the theorem is that $F=0$. We will show this by checking that $F$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{pseudoargument}. First observe that $F$ sends a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ of nonunital henselian rings to a fiber sequence of spectra. To see this, we consider the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ F(I') \ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}} \ar[r] & F(I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & F(\overline{I}) \ar[d] \\ F(I') \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes \overline{I})/p . }\] Note that the right-hand square is homotopy cartesian, so the top row is a fiber sequence if and only if the bottom row is a fiber sequence. But the bottom row is a fiber sequence by Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision} applied to the homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I',I')\rightarrow (\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I, I')$. Next, we claim that if $I' \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is nilpotent, then $F(I') = 0$. This follows from Theorem~\ref{DGMthm} which shows that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I', I') = 0$. To complete the proof, i.e., to verify the conditions of Proposition~\ref{pseudoargument}, we need to check that \[ F( k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+) = 0, \] whenever $k$ is a prime field. We write $k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ for the henselization of the polynomial ring $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ at $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$, so $k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \subset k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ is the maximal ideal. Using Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision}, it suffices to show that the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$. There are two cases for this. If $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq p$, this follows from Gabber rigidity. If $\mathrm{char}(k) = p$, this follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I,I)$ by excision and verify the hypotheses of the axiomatic rigidity argument for $F(I)=K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I,I)/p$. Free algebras over prime fields are handled by Gabber rigidity and the characteristic $p$ proposition.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I$
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision}, it suffices to consider the case where $(R, I) = (\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ where $I$ is a nonunital henselian ring.
nodes.statement_short: Excision.

nodes.name: The functor $F$
nodes.statement: We now consider the functor \[ F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}, \quad F(I) = K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)/p. \] By Propositions~\ref{Kpscoh} and \ref{TCpscoh}, $F$ is a projectively pseudocoherent functor. Implicit here is the statement (due to Quillen) that the $K$-groups of $\mathbb{Z}$ are finitely generated, as are the mod $p$ homotopy groups of $\mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z})$ (both of which follow from evaluating the projectively pseudocoherent functors $I \mapsto K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I), \mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p$ at $I = 0$).
nodes.statement_short: Define $F(I)=K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I,I)/p$, projectively pseudocoherent.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: The assertion of the theorem is that $F=0$. We will show this by checking that $F$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{pseudoargument}.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the hypotheses of the axiomatic rigidity argument.

nodes.name: Exactness
nodes.statement: First observe that $F$ sends a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ of nonunital henselian rings to a fiber sequence of spectra. To see this, we consider the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ F(I') \ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}} \ar[r] & F(I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & F(\overline{I}) \ar[d] \\ F(I') \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes \overline{I})/p . }\] Note that the right-hand square is homotopy cartesian, so the top row is a fiber sequence if and only if the bottom row is a fiber sequence. But the bottom row is a fiber sequence by Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision} applied to the homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I',I')\rightarrow (\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I, I')$.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ sends short exact sequences to fiber sequences.

nodes.name: Comparison diagram
nodes.statement: To see this, we consider the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ F(I') \ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}} \ar[r] & F(I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & F(\overline{I}) \ar[d] \\ F(I') \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes \overline{I})/p . }\]
nodes.statement_short: Diagram comparing rows.

nodes.name: Cartesian square
nodes.statement: Note that the right-hand square is homotopy cartesian, so the top row is a fiber sequence if and only if the bottom row is a fiber sequence.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the bottom row.

nodes.name: Excision
nodes.statement: But the bottom row is a fiber sequence by Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision} applied to the homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I',I')\rightarrow (\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I, I')$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply excision for $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$.

nodes.name: Nilpotent ideals
nodes.statement: Next, we claim that if $I' \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is nilpotent, then $F(I') = 0$. This follows from Theorem~\ref{DGMthm} which shows that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I', I') = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy.

nodes.name: Free algebras over prime fields
nodes.statement: To complete the proof, i.e., to verify the conditions of Proposition~\ref{pseudoargument}, we need to check that \[ F( k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+) = 0, \] whenever $k$ is a prime field. We write $k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ for the henselization of the polynomial ring $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ at $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$, so $k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \subset k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ is the maximal ideal. Using Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision}, it suffices to show that the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to rigidity of $K^{\mathrm{inv}}$ for $k\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\to k$.

nodes.name: Two cases
nodes.statement: There are two cases for this. If $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq p$, this follows from Gabber rigidity. If $\mathrm{char}(k) = p$, this follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp}.
nodes.statement_short: Split by characteristic.

nodes.name: Characteristic $\neq p$
nodes.statement: If $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq p$, this follows from Gabber rigidity.
nodes.statement_short: Gabber rigidity.

nodes.name: Characteristic $p$
nodes.statement: If $\mathrm{char}(k) = p$, this follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp}.
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic $p$ rigidity proposition.

nodes.name: Relation to Gabber's proof of rigidity
nodes.statement: Recall that Gabber's proof \cite{gabber} of rigidity is cleanly separated into two halves: the first half reduces the general case to the case of henselizations of smooth algebras over a field at a rational point, and the second half proves that case. In our proof above, we only need to invoke the second half of Gabber's work, which is also covered by Gillet--Thomason \cite{GT}. However, our entire line of reasoning is in some sense modeled on the first half of Gabber's proof. (The exceptions are Proposition \ref{rigidity:henspaircharp}, which is the new characteristic $p$ ingredient, and the commutation of $\mathrm{TC}/p$ with filtered colimits, which is a necessary technical statement.) So we are not really avoiding the first half of Gabber's proof, just explicating it in a modified context. Let us note in particular that the projective pseudocoherence of $K$-theory is our replacement for Suslin's ``method of universal homotopies" from \cite{Suslinlocal}, which has been crucial to many of the known rigidity results in $K$-theory.

nodes.name: Easier proof for $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras
nodes.statement: While the the full strength of pseudocoherence appears to be necessary to obtain results for $\mathbb{Z}$-algebras, the result for henselian pairs of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp} and the observation that $K, \mathrm{TC}/p$ commutes with filtered colimits of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras. One can then extend the result to $\mathbb{Z}_p$-algebras using the $p$-adic continuity statement of \cite{GHlocal} (and a similar filtered colimit argument). Thus, for $\mathbb{Z}_p$-algebras at least, one can prove the main result purely using the classical approach to $\mathrm{TC}$ and ingredients predating \cite{nikolaus-scholze}.
nodes.label: rem:fpcaseeasier

nodes.name: Failure of integral rigidity
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{mainthm} is false integrally; that is, the integral Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy theorem does not hold for henselian pairs. As an example, let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be a henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra with residue field $\mathbb{F}_p$. Then $\mathrm{TC}(R), \mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ are $p$-complete spectra, so $\mathrm{TC}_1(R, \mathfrak{m})$ is a derived $p$-adically complete abelian group. However, $K_1(R, \mathfrak{m}) =\mathrm{ker}(R^{\times} \to \mathbb{F}_p^{\times})$ which will essentially never be derived $p$-complete. For instance, consider the power series ring $R_0 = \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$ and let $R = (R_0)_{\mathrm{perf}}$ be the perfection of $R_0$. We have a surjection $R \to \mathbb{F}_p$, whose kernel is the henselian ideal $I = \bigcup (x^{1/p^n})$. In this case, $\mathrm{ker}(R^{\times} \to \mathbb{F}_p^{\times})$ is a nonzero $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$-module, which in particular is not derived $p$-complete.
nodes.statement_short: Rigidity fails integrally: for the perfection of $\mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$, $K_1$ relative is a nonzero $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$-module while relative TC is $p$-complete.

nodes.name: Continuity question in algebraic K-theory
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $I$ be an ideal. How close is the map \begin{equation} K(R) \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s) \end{equation} to being an equivalence?

nodes.name: Continuity map for K-theory
nodes.statement: K(R) \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s)
nodes.label: contmap

nodes.name: Continuity of K reduces to continuity of TC
nodes.statement: In order to apply our earlier results to this question, we observe that if $(R, I)$ is a henselian pair then Theorem~\ref{mainthm} implies that the map \eqref{contmap} becomes an equivalence modulo $p$ if and only if the corresponding map $\mathrm{TC}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$.
conclusions: the map \eqref{contmap} becomes an equivalence modulo $p$ if and only if the corresponding map $\mathrm{TC}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
equivalent_conditions: the map \eqref{contmap} becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
the corresponding map $\mathrm{TC}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$

nodes.name: $F$-finite $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra
nodes.statement: An $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$ is said to be \emph{$F$-finite} if the absolute Frobenius map $R \to R$ is finite, in other words if $R$ is a finitely generated module over its subring of $p^\sub{th}$-powers.
differentia: the absolute Frobenius map $R \to R$ is finite
nodes.label: Ffinite

nodes.name: THH and mod $p$ equivalences of rings
nodes.statement: Let $R \to R'$ be a map of commutative rings such that the map $R \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p \to R' \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p$ is an equivalence. Then $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(R')$ is a mod $p$ equivalence.
assumptions: $R \to R'$ be a map of commutative rings such that the map $R \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p \to R' \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p$ is an equivalence
conclusions: $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(R')$ is a mod $p$ equivalence
nodes.label: modplemma0

nodes.name: Proof of THH and mod $p$ equivalences of rings
nodes.statement: The hypothesis is equivalent to saying that $HR\rightarrow HR'$ is a mod $p$ equivalence of spectra. It follows that $(HR)^{\otimes n}\rightarrow (HR')^{\otimes n}$ is a mod $p$ equivalence for all $n\geq 0$, and hence that $\mathrm{THH}(R)\rightarrow \mathrm{THH}(R')$ is a mod $p$ equivalence, since mod $p$ equivalences are preserved under colimits.
nodes.statement_short: Mod $p$ equivalences are preserved by smash powers and colimits.

nodes.name: THH of a noetherian ring versus its $p$-completion
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring and let $\widehat{R}_p$ be its $p$-adic completion (which is also the derived $p$-adic completion, as $R$ has bounded $p$-power torsion). Then the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)$ is a mod $p$ equivalence.
conclusions: the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)$ is a mod $p$ equivalence
nodes.label: modplemma

nodes.name: Proof of THH of a noetherian ring versus its $p$-completion
nodes.statement: A noetherian ring has bounded $p$-torsion, which implies that the map $R \to \widehat{R}_p$ induces an equivalence $R \otimes^{\mathbb L}_\mathbb Z \mathbb{F}_p \simeq \widehat{R}_p \otimes^{\mathbb L}_\mathbb Z \mathbb{F}_p$. Thus the statement follows from Lemma \ref{modplemma0}.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded torsion gives a derived mod $p$ equivalence; apply the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Continuity of THH modulo $p$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I\subseteq R$, and suppose that $R/pR$ is $F$-finite. Then the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$.
assumptions: $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I\subseteq R$
conclusions: the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$
nodes.label: THHcont

nodes.name: Proof of Continuity of THH modulo $p$
nodes.statement: First we note that $\widehat R_p = \varprojlim_s \widehat{R/I^s}_p$ and $\widehat{R/I^s}_p = \widehat R_p /I^s\widehat R_p$. Indeed, $R$ being noetherian, we have that on finitely generated $R$-modules the $p$-adic completion identifies with the derived $p$-completion. It therefore preserves short exact sequences and sequential inverse limits along surjective transition maps, as these are examples of derived limits. In particular, $\widehat R_p$ is $I\widehat R_p$-adically complete. Therefore, the canonical map \[ \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)/p \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}( \widehat{R}_p/I^s \widehat{R}_p)/p\] is an equivalence by \cite[Thm.~4.5]{DundasMorrow}. But by the above, each quotient $\widehat R_p/I^s\widehat R_p$ coincides with the $p$-adic completion of $R/I^s$, so that applying Lemma~\ref{modplemma} to $R$ and to each $R/I^s $ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the $p$-complete case and apply Dundas--Morrow continuity.

nodes.name: Completion commutes
nodes.statement: First we note that $\widehat R_p = \varprojlim_s \widehat{R/I^s}_p$ and $\widehat{R/I^s}_p = \widehat R_p /I^s\widehat R_p$. Indeed, $R$ being noetherian, we have that on finitely generated $R$-modules the $p$-adic completion identifies with the derived $p$-completion. It therefore preserves short exact sequences and sequential inverse limits along surjective transition maps, as these are examples of derived limits.
nodes.statement_short: $p$-completion commutes with $I$-adic limits for noetherian $R$.

nodes.name: Dundas--Morrow
nodes.statement: In particular, $\widehat R_p$ is $I\widehat R_p$-adically complete. Therefore, the canonical map \[ \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)/p \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}( \widehat{R}_p/I^s \widehat{R}_p)/p\] is an equivalence by \cite[Thm.~4.5]{DundasMorrow}.
nodes.statement_short: THH continuity for the $p$-complete ring.

nodes.name: Compare with $R$
nodes.statement: But by the above, each quotient $\widehat R_p/I^s\widehat R_p$ coincides with the $p$-adic completion of $R/I^s$, so that applying Lemma~\ref{modplemma} to $R$ and to each $R/I^s $ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $p$-completion lemma.

nodes.name: Continuity of K-theory modulo $p$ for complete noetherian rings
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I$, and suppose that $R/pR$ is $F$-finite. Then the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$.
assumptions: $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I$
conclusions: the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$
also_stated_at: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring and $I \subset R$ an ideal. Suppose $R$ is $I$-adically complete and $R/p$ is $F$-finite. Then the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim K(R/I^n)$ is a $p$-adic equivalence.
nodes.label: Kcont

nodes.name: Proof of Continuity of K-theory modulo $p$ for complete noetherian rings
nodes.statement: Using Theorem~\ref{mainthm}, the result reduces to the statement that $\mathrm{TC}(R)/p \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)/p$ is an equivalence. By Remark~\ref{TCinvlim}, this in turn follows from the analogous statement for $\mathrm{THH}$, which is given by Proposition~\ref{THHcont}.
nodes.statement_short: Main theorem reduces to TC; pass to THH and apply THH continuity.

nodes.name: Continuity is equivalent to the main theorem
nodes.statement: One can see that Theorem~\ref{Kcont} is in fact equivalent to Theorem~\ref{mainthm} (our main theorem on henselian pairs). Indeed, suppose Theorem~\ref{Kcont} is known, and let $(R,I)$ be a henselian pair. We want to show that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p\rightarrow K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$ is an equivalence. Since $K$ and $\mathrm{TC}/p$ commute with filtered colimits, so does $K^{\mathrm{inv}}/p$, hence we can assume $(R,I)$ is the henselization of a finite type $\mathbb{Z}$-algebra at an ideal. Let $\widehat{R}$ denote the $I$-adic completion of $R$. By N\'eron--Popescu desingularization \cite{Popescu1, Popescu2} (see also \cite[Tag 07BW]{stacks-project}), applicable in view of the geometric regularity of $R \to \widehat{R}$ (see \cite[7.8.3(v)]{EGA_IV_2}), the map $R\rightarrow \widehat{R}$ is ind-smooth, i.e., we can write $\widehat{R}$ as a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras. Given a smooth $R$-algebra $A$ and a map $A \to \widehat{R}$ of $R$-algebras, it follows that the map $R \to A$ admits a section by Elkik's theorem (Theorem~\ref{elkikthm}). Therefore, we deduce that $R\rightarrow \widehat{R}$ is a filtered colimit of split injections. Thus the claim for $(R,I)$ (i.e., that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$ is an equivalence) will follow from the claim for $(\widehat{R}, I \widehat{R})$. (This is a standard Artin approximation argument.) However, by the above continuity in $K$ and $\mathrm{TC}$, we have $$K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\widehat{R})/p\overset{\simeq}{\rightarrow}\varprojlim K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I^n)/p.$$ On the other hand, the right hand side is a constant limit with value $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$, by Theorem~\ref{DGMthm}. This gives the claim for $(\widehat{R}, I\widehat{R})$, and therefore in general, by the above argument.
nodes.statement_short: Derives the main theorem from continuity via N\'eron--Popescu, Elkik lifting and the Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy theorem.
nodes.label: henspairequivtocontinuity

nodes.name: Failure of continuity for non-$F$-finite fields
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be an field of characteristic $p$ which is not $F$-finite, i.e., any $p$-basis\footnote{We refer to \cite[\S26]{Matsumura1989} for a reminder on the notion of a $p$-basis, including the fact that a collection of elements $\{b_i\}$ of $k$ forms part of a $p$-basis if and only if their differentials $\{db_i\}$ are linearly independent in $\Omega^1_k$.} of $k$ has infinite cardinality. Then the map $K(k[[t]])/p \to \varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not an equivalence; more precisely, the map on $\pi_2$ is not surjective.
nodes.statement_short: If $k$ has infinite $p$-basis, $K(k[[t]])/p\to\varprojlim K(k[t]/t^s)/p$ is not surjective on $\pi_2$.
assumptions: $k$ be an field of characteristic $p$ which is not $F$-finite
conclusions: the map $K(k[[t]])/p \to \varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not an equivalence
the map on $\pi_2$ is not surjective

nodes.name: Proof of Failure of continuity for non-$F$-finite fields
nodes.statement: We begin with several straightforward reductions to Milnor $K$-theory. Firstly, since $k[[t]]^\times$ is $p$-torsion-free, the canonical map $K_2(k[[t]])/p\to \pi_2 (K(k[[t]])/p)$ is an isomorphism. The $p$-torsion in the pro abelian group $\{k[t]/(t^s)^\times\}_s$ is also zero, since the transition map $k[t]/(t^{ps})^\times\to k[t]/(t^s)^\times$ clearly kills all $p$-torsion in the domain, and therefore $\{K_2(k[t]/(t^s))/p\}_s\to \{\pi_2(K(k[t]/(t^s))/p) \}_s$ is an isomorphism of pro abelian groups. Secondly, $k[[t]]$ and $k[t]/(t^s)$ are local rings with infinite residue field, whence a classical result in algebraic $K$-theory \cite[\S8]{vanderKallen1977} states that $K_2^M(k[[t]])\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[[t]])$ and $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[t]/(t^s))$. Finally, the canonical map $\pi_2 (\varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)\to \varprojlim_s\pi_2( K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)$ is surjective, by the Milnor sequence. In conclusion, to prove the theorem it is sufficient to show that the canonical map $K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\to\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not surjective. To do this, we will detect symbols using the $\mathrm{dlog}$ maps from $K_2^M$ to absolute K\"ahler differentials $\Omega^2_{-}:=\Omega^2_{-/\mathbb F_p}$: \[\xymatrix{ \Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\ar[r]&\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\\ K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\ar[u]_{\operatorname{dlog}}\ar[r] &\varprojlim_s K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p\ar[u]_{\operatorname{dlog}} }\] It remains to construct an element in the bottom right of the diagram whose image in the top right does not come from the top left. We now closely follow Bloch--Esnault--Kerz, with the necessary modifications to deal with the fact that we will eventually need to restrict to dlog forms. Given any map of rings $R\to S$ and differential form $\tau\in\Omega^2_{S/R}$, define its {\em weight} $w(\tau)$ to be the smallest integer $n$ for which it is possible to write $\tau=\sum_{i=1}^na_idb_i\wedge dc_i$ for some $a_i,b_i,c_i\in S$. If $\ell$ is a subfield of $k$ and $b_1,\dots,b_n,c_1,\dots,c_n\in k$ form part of a $p$-basis for $k$ relative to $\ell$, then the elements $d b_1,\dots,d b_n,d c_1,\dots,d c_n$ are linearly independent in the $k$-vector space $\Omega^1_{k/\ell}$ and so this element $\sum_{i=1}^ndb_i\wedge dc_i$ has weight $\ge n$ in $\Omega^2_{k/\ell}$ (Lemma~\ref{linalg} below). Next consider the derivation $$k[t]/(t^s) \rightarrow \Omega^1_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which ``holds $t$ constant", so $\sum_n c_n t^n \mapsto \sum_n (dc_n)t^n$. This extends by multiplicativity to a map $$\Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which splits the canonical map $\Omega^\ast_k\otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}$. Restricting to degree $\ast=2$ and passing to the limit as $s\to\infty$ defines \[e:\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s),\] where each element on the right may be expressed as $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_i t^i$ for some unique $\tau_0,\tau_1,\dots\in \Omega^2_k$ (the {\em $t$-adic coefficients} of the element). Bloch--Esnault--Kerz \cite[Lem.~B2]{BlochEsnaultKerz2013} show (assuming $k = \mathbb{C}$, but the argument works in general) that the image of the composition \[\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)\] lands inside the set of those elements $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_j t^j$ whose $t$-adic coefficients satisfy the following: there exists $N\ge0$ such that $w(\tau_j)\le N\binom{j+2}j$ for all $j\ge0$. We are now prepared to complete the proof by constructing a bad element of $\varprojlim_s K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$. First pick a sequence $0<w_1<w_2<\cdots$ of integers growing sufficiently fast such that no value of $N$ satisfies $w_j\le N\binom{2j}{2j-2}$ for all $j\ge1$. Then pick a sequence of subfields $\mathbb F_p=k_0\subset k_1\subset k_2\subset\cdots$ of $k$ such that any $p$-basis for $k_j$ relative to $k_{j-1}$ has $\ge2w_j$ elements; let $b_1^{(j)},\cdots,b_{w_j}^{(j)},c_1^{(j)},\cdots,c_{w_j}^{(j)}\in k_i$ be part of such a relative $p$-basis. Set \[f_s:=\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\sum_{i=1}^{w_j}\{1+t^jb_i^{(j)},1+t^jc_i^{(j)}\}\in K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\] and note that the transition map $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\to K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s-1}))/p$ exactly kills the $j=s-1$ part of the sum and therefore sends $f_s$ to $f_{s-1}$; we therefore may define $f:=\varprojlim_s f_s\in\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p$. Let $\sum_{i\ge 1}\tau_it^i$ be the expansion of $e(\mathrm{dlog} f)\in\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)$. Noting that \[\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jb)\wedge\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jc)\equiv t^{2j}da\wedge db\text{ mod }dt,\,t^{3j}\] with all the higher order terms given by various expressions in $b,c$, we see that \[\tau_{2s-2}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{w_{s}}b_i^{(s)}\wedge c_i^{(s)} \text{ mod }{\Omega^2_{k_{s-1}}}.\] By the second paragraph of the proof we deduce that the image of $\tau_{2s-2}$ in $\Omega^2_{k/k_{s-1}}$ has weight $\ge w_s$, whence a fortiori $w(\tau_{2s-2})\ge w_s$. By choice of the sequence $0< w_1<\cdots$, it follows that $\mathrm{dlog} f$ cannot be lifted to $\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Milnor $K_2$ and detect symbols via dlog forms. The key step builds an inverse system of symbols whose dlog weights grow too fast to lift to $k[[t]]$.

nodes.name: Reduce to Milnor $K_2$
nodes.statement: We begin with several straightforward reductions to Milnor $K$-theory. Firstly, since $k[[t]]^\times$ is $p$-torsion-free, the canonical map $K_2(k[[t]])/p\to \pi_2 (K(k[[t]])/p)$ is an isomorphism. The $p$-torsion in the pro abelian group $\{k[t]/(t^s)^\times\}_s$ is also zero, since the transition map $k[t]/(t^{ps})^\times\to k[t]/(t^s)^\times$ clearly kills all $p$-torsion in the domain, and therefore $\{K_2(k[t]/(t^s))/p\}_s\to \{\pi_2(K(k[t]/(t^s))/p) \}_s$ is an isomorphism of pro abelian groups. Secondly, $k[[t]]$ and $k[t]/(t^s)$ are local rings with infinite residue field, whence a classical result in algebraic $K$-theory \cite[\S8]{vanderKallen1977} states that $K_2^M(k[[t]])\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[[t]])$ and $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[t]/(t^s))$. Finally, the canonical map $\pi_2 (\varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)\to \varprojlim_s\pi_2( K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)$ is surjective, by the Milnor sequence. In conclusion, to prove the theorem it is sufficient to show that the canonical map $K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\to\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to non-surjectivity on Milnor $K_2$ mod $p$.

nodes.name: Torsion-freeness
nodes.statement: Firstly, since $k[[t]]^\times$ is $p$-torsion-free, the canonical map $K_2(k[[t]])/p\to \pi_2 (K(k[[t]])/p)$ is an isomorphism. The $p$-torsion in the pro abelian group $\{k[t]/(t^s)^\times\}_s$ is also zero, since the transition map $k[t]/(t^{ps})^\times\to k[t]/(t^s)^\times$ clearly kills all $p$-torsion in the domain, and therefore $\{K_2(k[t]/(t^s))/p\}_s\to \{\pi_2(K(k[t]/(t^s))/p) \}_s$ is an isomorphism of pro abelian groups.
nodes.statement_short: Units are $p$-torsion-free, so $K_2/p\cong\pi_2(K/p)$.

nodes.name: Milnor $K_2$
nodes.statement: Secondly, $k[[t]]$ and $k[t]/(t^s)$ are local rings with infinite residue field, whence a classical result in algebraic $K$-theory \cite[\S8]{vanderKallen1977} states that $K_2^M(k[[t]])\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[[t]])$ and $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[t]/(t^s))$.
nodes.statement_short: van der Kallen: $K_2^M\cong K_2$ for local rings with infinite residue field.

nodes.name: Milnor sequence
nodes.statement: Finally, the canonical map $\pi_2 (\varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)\to \varprojlim_s\pi_2( K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)$ is surjective, by the Milnor sequence. In conclusion, to prove the theorem it is sufficient to show that the canonical map $K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\to\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Milnor $K_2$ modulo $p$.

nodes.name: dlog detection
nodes.statement: To do this, we will detect symbols using the $\mathrm{dlog}$ maps from $K_2^M$ to absolute K\"ahler differentials $\Omega^2_{-}:=\Omega^2_{-/\mathbb F_p}$: \[\xymatrix{ \Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\ar[r]&\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\\ K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\ar[u]_{\operatorname{dlog}}\ar[r] &\varprojlim_s K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p\ar[u]_{\operatorname{dlog}} }\] It remains to construct an element in the bottom right of the diagram whose image in the top right does not come from the top left.
nodes.statement_short: Detect via dlog to $\Omega^2$.

nodes.name: Weight of forms
nodes.statement: We now closely follow Bloch--Esnault--Kerz, with the necessary modifications to deal with the fact that we will eventually need to restrict to dlog forms. Given any map of rings $R\to S$ and differential form $\tau\in\Omega^2_{S/R}$, define its {\em weight} $w(\tau)$ to be the smallest integer $n$ for which it is possible to write $\tau=\sum_{i=1}^na_idb_i\wedge dc_i$ for some $a_i,b_i,c_i\in S$. If $\ell$ is a subfield of $k$ and $b_1,\dots,b_n,c_1,\dots,c_n\in k$ form part of a $p$-basis for $k$ relative to $\ell$, then the elements $d b_1,\dots,d b_n,d c_1,\dots,d c_n$ are linearly independent in the $k$-vector space $\Omega^1_{k/\ell}$ and so this element $\sum_{i=1}^ndb_i\wedge dc_i$ has weight $\ge n$ in $\Omega^2_{k/\ell}$ (Lemma~\ref{linalg} below).
nodes.statement_short: Define weight; independent $p$-basis elements give large weight.

nodes.name: Map $e$ and $t$-adic coefficients
nodes.statement: Next consider the derivation $$k[t]/(t^s) \rightarrow \Omega^1_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which ``holds $t$ constant", so $\sum_n c_n t^n \mapsto \sum_n (dc_n)t^n$. This extends by multiplicativity to a map $$\Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which splits the canonical map $\Omega^\ast_k\otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}$. Restricting to degree $\ast=2$ and passing to the limit as $s\to\infty$ defines \[e:\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s),\] where each element on the right may be expressed as $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_i t^i$ for some unique $\tau_0,\tau_1,\dots\in \Omega^2_k$ (the {\em $t$-adic coefficients} of the element). Bloch--Esnault--Kerz \cite[Lem.~B2]{BlochEsnaultKerz2013} show (assuming $k = \mathbb{C}$, but the argument works in general) that the image of the composition \[\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)\] lands inside the set of those elements $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_j t^j$ whose $t$-adic coefficients satisfy the following: there exists $N\ge0$ such that $w(\tau_j)\le N\binom{j+2}j$ for all $j\ge0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bloch--Esnault--Kerz bound on weights of coefficients from $k[[t]]$.

nodes.name: Derivation holding $t$ constant
nodes.statement: Next consider the derivation $$k[t]/(t^s) \rightarrow \Omega^1_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which ``holds $t$ constant", so $\sum_n c_n t^n \mapsto \sum_n (dc_n)t^n$. This extends by multiplicativity to a map $$\Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which splits the canonical map $\Omega^\ast_k\otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Split map of forms.

nodes.name: Map $e$
nodes.statement: Restricting to degree $\ast=2$ and passing to the limit as $s\to\infty$ defines \[e:\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s),\] where each element on the right may be expressed as $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_i t^i$ for some unique $\tau_0,\tau_1,\dots\in \Omega^2_k$ (the {\em $t$-adic coefficients} of the element).
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit.

nodes.name: Weight bound
nodes.statement: Bloch--Esnault--Kerz \cite[Lem.~B2]{BlochEsnaultKerz2013} show (assuming $k = \mathbb{C}$, but the argument works in general) that the image of the composition \[\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)\] lands inside the set of those elements $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_j t^j$ whose $t$-adic coefficients satisfy the following: there exists $N\ge0$ such that $w(\tau_j)\le N\binom{j+2}j$ for all $j\ge0$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients from $k[[t]]$ have polynomially bounded weight.

nodes.name: Bad element
nodes.statement: We are now prepared to complete the proof by constructing a bad element of $\varprojlim_s K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$. First pick a sequence $0<w_1<w_2<\cdots$ of integers growing sufficiently fast such that no value of $N$ satisfies $w_j\le N\binom{2j}{2j-2}$ for all $j\ge1$. Then pick a sequence of subfields $\mathbb F_p=k_0\subset k_1\subset k_2\subset\cdots$ of $k$ such that any $p$-basis for $k_j$ relative to $k_{j-1}$ has $\ge2w_j$ elements; let $b_1^{(j)},\cdots,b_{w_j}^{(j)},c_1^{(j)},\cdots,c_{w_j}^{(j)}\in k_i$ be part of such a relative $p$-basis. Set \[f_s:=\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\sum_{i=1}^{w_j}\{1+t^jb_i^{(j)},1+t^jc_i^{(j)}\}\in K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\] and note that the transition map $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\to K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s-1}))/p$ exactly kills the $j=s-1$ part of the sum and therefore sends $f_s$ to $f_{s-1}$; we therefore may define $f:=\varprojlim_s f_s\in\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $f$ from rapidly growing families of $p$-basis symbols.

nodes.name: Growth sequence
nodes.statement: First pick a sequence $0<w_1<w_2<\cdots$ of integers growing sufficiently fast such that no value of $N$ satisfies $w_j\le N\binom{2j}{2j-2}$ for all $j\ge1$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $w_j$ growing too fast.

nodes.name: Subfields and $p$-bases
nodes.statement: Then pick a sequence of subfields $\mathbb F_p=k_0\subset k_1\subset k_2\subset\cdots$ of $k$ such that any $p$-basis for $k_j$ relative to $k_{j-1}$ has $\ge2w_j$ elements; let $b_1^{(j)},\cdots,b_{w_j}^{(j)},c_1^{(j)},\cdots,c_{w_j}^{(j)}\in k_i$ be part of such a relative $p$-basis.
nodes.statement_short: Choose relative $p$-bases of size $\geq 2w_j$.

nodes.name: Compatible symbols
nodes.statement: Set \[f_s:=\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\sum_{i=1}^{w_j}\{1+t^jb_i^{(j)},1+t^jc_i^{(j)}\}\in K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\] and note that the transition map $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\to K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s-1}))/p$ exactly kills the $j=s-1$ part of the sum and therefore sends $f_s$ to $f_{s-1}$; we therefore may define $f:=\varprojlim_s f_s\in\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p$.
nodes.statement_short: Define compatible $f_s$ and $f$.

nodes.name: Weights too large
nodes.statement: Let $\sum_{i\ge 1}\tau_it^i$ be the expansion of $e(\mathrm{dlog} f)\in\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)$. Noting that \[\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jb)\wedge\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jc)\equiv t^{2j}da\wedge db\text{ mod }dt,\,t^{3j}\] with all the higher order terms given by various expressions in $b,c$, we see that \[\tau_{2s-2}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{w_{s}}b_i^{(s)}\wedge c_i^{(s)} \text{ mod }{\Omega^2_{k_{s-1}}}.\] By the second paragraph of the proof we deduce that the image of $\tau_{2s-2}$ in $\Omega^2_{k/k_{s-1}}$ has weight $\ge w_s$, whence a fortiori $w(\tau_{2s-2})\ge w_s$. By choice of the sequence $0< w_1<\cdots$, it follows that $\mathrm{dlog} f$ cannot be lifted to $\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients of $e(\mathrm{dlog} f)$ have unbounded weight, so no lift.

nodes.name: Compute coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $\sum_{i\ge 1}\tau_it^i$ be the expansion of $e(\mathrm{dlog} f)\in\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)$. Noting that \[\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jb)\wedge\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jc)\equiv t^{2j}da\wedge db\text{ mod }dt,\,t^{3j}\] with all the higher order terms given by various expressions in $b,c$, we see that \[\tau_{2s-2}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{w_{s}}b_i^{(s)}\wedge c_i^{(s)} \text{ mod }{\Omega^2_{k_{s-1}}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Leading term of $\tau_{2s-2}$.

nodes.name: Weight bound
nodes.statement: By the second paragraph of the proof we deduce that the image of $\tau_{2s-2}$ in $\Omega^2_{k/k_{s-1}}$ has weight $\ge w_s$, whence a fortiori $w(\tau_{2s-2})\ge w_s$.
nodes.statement_short: $w(\tau_{2s-2})\geq w_s$.

nodes.name: Contradiction with BEK bound
nodes.statement: By choice of the sequence $0< w_1<\cdots$, it follows that $\mathrm{dlog} f$ cannot be lifted to $\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mathrm{dlog} f$ does not lift.
